## pqac-00000000

From text 'benedettiUnknownyeardataanalyticsfor pages 42-46'.

A Benedetti. Data analytics for powder feeding modelling on continuous secondary pharmaceutical manufacturing processes. Unknown journal, Unknown year.

The excerpt describes a loss-in-weight feeder whose primary measured signal is total feeder, hopper, and powder weight versus time. The derivative of weight loss provides the fed mass-flow rate, which is compared with a target; the controller adjusts motor/screw speed. During hopper refill, the load cell becomes effectively unavailable, so volumetric control or an inferred feed-factor-based strategy is used. The feed factor is defined as outlet mass flow rate divided by screw velocity (mass per screw revolution), making screw speed the manipulated/input variable and mass flow the controlled/output variable during normal gravimetric operation. The text interprets feed factor as an indirect indicator of powder density: higher mass per revolution implies higher density. Refill can compact the residual powder, increasing density and causing overfeeding, reported as approximately +1% to +10–15% depending on material. The excerpt discusses density, flow properties, hopper level, and feed-rate error, but does not describe particle size or particle-size distribution as an explicitly estimated output from balance weight-time data, feed fluctuations, mass per revolution, or feed factor. It also contains no discussion of Li, Bostijn, Yang, Fathollahi, or Hou, and no inversion from feeder measurements to particle-size output is specified.

## pqac-00000001

From text 'li2020predictiveperformanceof pages 44-49'.

Tianyi Li. Predictive performance of loss-in-weight feeders for continuous powder-based manufacturing. ArXiv, Jan 2020. URL: https://doi.org/10.7282/t3-6tgx-8f63, doi:10.7282/t3-6tgx-8f63. This article has 2 citations.

This excerpt from Li (2020) does not describe particle size or particle-size distribution being estimated as an output from balance weight-versus-time, feed-mass fluctuations, mass per screw revolution, or feed factor. Instead, the direction is primarily material properties and screw/operating conditions → feeder performance. Material characterization includes bulk density, compressibility, tapped density, Hausner ratio, cohesion, and flow function; these properties are examined for their effects on operational flow-rate range. The measured balance mass change over a time interval is converted into actual mass feed rate, ṁᵢ = Δmᵢ/Δt. Those feed-rate measurements are then used to calculate RSD and RDM, which are outputs describing dosing precision and setpoint deviation, not particle size. Feed factor is likewise an operational calibration quantity: the feeder runs for 30 seconds at 50% drive command, and mass change is used to calculate the feed factor, defined as flow rate at 100% drive command. The study reports correlations between material flow properties, density, screw type, drive command, and feed-rate stability. It identifies higher RSD at low and very high drive commands and recommends 40–90% drive command. No inversion from feeder signals to particle size, no particle-size estimator, and no explicit particle-size-distribution output is reported in this excerpt.

The inputs (X) were 25 precharacterized material-property descriptors; the outputs (Y) were feeder-performance responses. In volumetric mode, the measured/derived outputs were maximum feed factor (FFmax) and feed-factor decay (FFdecay), reflecting feeding capacity and hopper-fill dependence. In gravimetric mode, the outputs were feed-rate variability (RSD) and setpoint-to-mean-feed-rate error (RE). PLS models predicted these feeding responses from the material descriptors, and two new powders were used for validation. The excerpt does not identify which descriptors represented particle size, does not report a size-distribution inversion, and does not claim that particle size was reconstructed from feeder signals. It also does not provide information about Li, Yang, Fathollahi, or Hou, so no cross-paper comparison or physical correlation for those studies can be supported from this source. Bostijn’s stated physical interpretation is that gravimetric control reduces the influence of material properties, whereas volumetric responses retain stronger material-property dependence.

The feeder experiments measured mass flow rates for 14 materials using four screw types and six feed rates. The principal feeder operating variable was drive command (motor speed), with an effective range reported as 20–90%. The feed factor was defined as the maximum mass flow rate for a particular material, feeder, and screw combination at 100% drive command. The reported physical correlation was between conditioned bulk density—used as an indicator of powder packing—and feed factor. Thus, the direction described is material characterization (especially conditioned bulk density) plus feeder/screw settings to predict or calculate maximum flow and effective mass-flow ranges. It is not an inverse model from feeder measurements to particle size. Abstract:
Abstract: Background: Precise continuous feeding of active pharmaceutical ingredients (APIs) and excipients is crucial in a continuous powder-to-tablet manufacturing setup, as any inconsistency can affect the final tablet quality. Method: This study investigated the impact of various materials on the performance of a continuous twin-screw loss-in-weight (LIW) feeder. The materials tested included spray-dried lactose, anhydrous lactose, granulated lactose, microcrystalline cellulose (MCC), an MCC–lactose preblend (50%:50% w/w ratio), and a co-processed excipient (lactose–lactitol at a 95%:5% w/w ratio). The feeding performance of these excipients was systematically assessed, focusing on powder densification and screw layering within the LIW feeder. Results: The results demonstrated densification for the spray-dried lactose and preblend. Densification was more pronounced during the initial feeding cycles for spray-dried lactose, but decreased gradually over time. In contrast, the densification remained relatively constant throughout the feeding process for the preblend. Notably, minor screw layering was observed for both spray-dried lactose and anhydrous lactose, with the extent of this issue reducing over time for the spray-dried lactose. Interestingly, granulated lactose grades did not show screw layering, making them preferable for blending with APIs prone to severe screw layering. The LIW feeder control system successfully managed powder densification and minor screw layering, maintaining the mass flow rate at the set point for all investigated materials. Conclusions: These findings inform the selection of optimal excipients, appropriate tooling for LIW feeders, and the enhancement of control strategies to shorten startup times. By addressing these factors, the precision and reliability of continuous feeding processes can be improved.

Abstract:
Abstract. The Cape Verde Atmospheric Observatory (CVAO), which is influenced by both marine and desert dust air masses, has been used for long-term measurements of different properties of the atmospheric aerosol from 2008 to 2017. These properties include particle number size distributions (PNSD), light-absorbing carbon (LAC) and concentrations of cloud condensation nuclei (CCN) together with their hygroscopicity. Here we summarize the results obtained for these properties and use an unsupervised machine learning algorithm for the classification of aerosol types. Five types of aerosols, i.e., marine, freshly formed, mixture, moderate dust and heavy dust, were classified. Air masses during marine periods are from the Atlantic Ocean and during dust periods are from the Sahara Desert. Heavy dust was more frequently present during wintertime, whereas the clean marine periods were more frequently present during springtime. It was observed that during the dust periods CCN number concentrations at a supersaturation of 0.30 % were roughly 2.5 times higher than during marine periods, but the hygroscopicity (κ) of particles in the size range from ∼ 30 to ∼ 175 nm during marine and dust periods were comparable. The long-term data presented here, together with the aerosol classification, can be used as a basis to improve our understanding of annual cycles of the atmospheric aerosol in the eastern tropical Atlantic Ocean and on aerosol-cloud interactions and it can be used as a basis for driving, evaluating and constraining atmospheric model simulations.

Abstract:
Although large amounts of research have been completed to find the relationship between particulate matter and climate change, they have still proven to be inadequate. Efforts to lay the foundations for understanding atmospheric chemical reactions have been repeatedly foiled by both the size and complexity of the task, which require more than the effort of a handful of researchers. Since the development of advanced physical models for dust behavior is projected to take years, what if laypeople could dramatically expedite this process by using their mobile devices as measurement tools? With relatively little effort by many individuals, previously unknown information about the earth’s atmosphere may at last become accessible thanks to recent advances in artificial intelligence. However, there are potential obstacles. Even if all technical problems are resolved, viable plans for battling particulate matter pollution will likely need to be accompanied by environmental policies. While technological breakthroughs give reason to hope for a brighter future, the resolution of global issues requires both grassroots changes and global efforts.

Abstract:
Segregation is a common problem in batch-based direct compression (BDC) processes, especially with low-dose tablet products, as is the preparation of a homogenous mixture. The scope of the current work was to explore if a continuous direct compression (CDC) process could serve as a solution for these challenges. Furthermore, the principle of a platform formulation was demonstrated for low dose tablets. The combination of filler excipients and the API in the formulation used was suitable for direct compression, but also prone to induce segregation in BDC process. The CDC process was found to be very promising; it was shown that tablets with the desired quality parameters could be manufactured successfully with both of the APIs studied. Powder analysis indicated that the APIs display some fundamental differences in their physical properties, which was also reflected in powder mixture properties and, hence, eventually in processing. However, process parameters, especially mixer impeller speed, were not found to have any significant influence on end product quality. The study suggests that a CDC process can be a viable solution to resolve the challenges described. Moreover, manufacturing by using a universal platform formulation seems to be a feasible way for producing low-dose tablets.

Abstract:
Moisture of bulk material has a significant impact on energetic efficiency of dry grinding, resultant particle size distribution and particle shape, and conditions of powder transport. As a consequence, moisture needs to be measured or estimated (modelled) in many points. This research investigates mutual relations between material moisture and particle classification process in a grinding installation. The experimental setup involves an inertial-impingement classifier and cyclone being part of dry grinding circuit with electromagnetic mill and recycle of coarse particles. The tested granular material is copper ore of particle size 0–1.25 mm and relative moisture content 0.5–5%, fed to the installation at various rates. Higher moisture of input material is found to change the operation of the classifier. Computed correlation coefficients show increased content of fine particles in lower product of classification. Additionally, drying of lower and upper classification products with respect to moisture of input material is modelled. Straight line models with and without saturation are estimated with recursive least squares method accounting for measurement errors in both predictor and response variables. These simple models are intended for use in automatic control system of the grinding installation.

Abstract:
Twin-screw granulation has emerged as a key process in powder processing industries and in the pharmaceutical sector to produce granules with controlled properties. This comprehensive review provides an overview of the simulation techniques and approaches that have been employed in the study of twin-screw granulation processes. This review discusses the major aspects of the twin-screw granulation process which include the fundamental principles of twin-screw granulation, equipment design, process parameters, and simulation methodologies. It highlights the importance of operating conditions and formulation designs in powder flow dynamics, mixing behaviour, and particle interactions within the twin-screw granulator for enhancing product quality and process efficiency. Simulation techniques such as the population balance model (PBM), computational fluid dynamics (CFD), the discrete element method (DEM), process modelling software (PMS), and other coupled techniques are critically discussed with a focus on simulating twin-screw granulation processes. This paper examines the challenges and limitations associated with each simulation approach and provides insights into future research directions. Overall, this article serves as a valuable resource for researchers who intend to develop their understanding of twin-screw granulation and provides insights into the various techniques and approaches available for simulating the twin-screw granulation process.

Abstract:
This paper proposes a feed rate control strategy for a novel volumetric micro-feeder, which can accomplish low-dose feeding of pharmaceutical raw materials with significantly different powder properties. The developed feed-forward control strategy enables a constant feed rate with a minimum deviation from the set-point, even for materials that are typically difficult to accurately feed (e.g., due to high cohesion or low density) using conventional continuous feeders. Density variations observed during the feeding process were characterized via a displacement feed factor profile for each powder. The characterized effective displacement density profile was applied in the micro-feeder system to proactively control the feed rate by manipulating the powder displacement rate (i.e., computing the feed rate from the powder displacement rate). Based on the displacement feed factor profile, the feed rate can be predicted during the feeding process and at any feed rate set-point. Three pharmaceutically relevant materials were used for the micro-feeder evaluation: di-calcium phosphate (large-particle system, high density), croscarmellose sodium (small-particle system, medium density), and barium sulfate (very small-particle <10 μm, high density). A significant improvement in the feeding performance was achieved for all investigated materials. The feed rate deviation from the set-point and its relative standard deviation were minimal compared to operations without the control strategy.

Abstract:
Purpose Continuous wet granulation and drying require an adequate process control strategy to ensure the product quality. The most important critical quality attributes of dried granules are the granule size distribution and moisture content. Process analytical technologies (PATs) are available for real-time monitoring of moisture content by, e.g., near-infrared spectroscopy (NIRS), which requires additional installation and complex multivariate validation. Thus, a mass and energy balance (MEB) was derived for a vibrated fluidised bed dryer, which is part of the QbCon^® 1 intended for continuous wet granulation and drying. Method Process parameters that are frequently logged were used for the derivation of a MEB. The predicted MEB was compared with the measured loss-on-drying (LOD) for two different formulations. Results The model-derived data were in good agreement with the observed LOD, leading to RMSE values of 0.12–0.45. Conclusion The implemented MEB can predict the LOD over time and thus might be suitable as a soft sensor without the installation of additional sensors. The obtained energy flux gives insight into the heat transfer, and the derived energy balance might be used to determine the required energy under certain drying conditions.

Abstract:
The purpose of this manuscript is to demonstrate that implementation of gravimetric measurements provides the same assurance of product quality and process control as spectroscopic measurements (1) for control of drug content in a fixed-dose combination (FDC) tablet and (2) for identification of non-conforming material. A wet granulation continuous tableting line was used to make the FDC drug product batches. Comparative data was generated for ten batches using near-infrared (NIR) spectroscopy for core tablets, and gravimetric in-process control measurements (IPCs) applied to the ratio control of intra- and extra-granular blend (IG and EG). HPLC reference data were collected to further demonstrate uniformity at each stage of the production process, including IG, final blend, and core tablets. All possible sources of variation not directly detectable by the gravimetric measurements were considered and quantified. The two IPC measurement techniques showed excellent agreement where both were within 2% of the target drug concentrations and within 2% of each other for the ten comparative batches. The NIR was more sensitive to material and process variations than the gravimetric IPCs; thus, it was more variable within and across batches. Gravimetric IPCs were demonstrated as an effective replacement for spectroscopic measurements for continuous tableting operations, capable of ensuring on target manufacturing and detection of non-conforming material. As pharmaceutical companies continue to push toward operational simplicity and sustainable manufacturing processes, soft-sensor and gravimetric controls as alternatives to their spectroscopic counterparts will be applied more broadly for process monitoring and control.

Abstract:
Highly potent active pharmaceutical ingredients (APIs) and low-dose excipients, or excipients with very low density, are notoriously hard to feed with currently available commercial technology. The micro-feeder system presented in this work is capable of feeding low-dose rates of powders with different particle sizes and flow properties. Two different grades of lactose, di-calcium phosphate, croscarmellose sodium, silicon dioxide, a spray-dried intermediate, and an active ingredient were studied to vary material properties to test performance of the system. The current micro-feeder system is a volumetric feeder combined with a weighing balance at the outlet that measures feeder output rates. Feeding results are shown as a so-called “displacement-feed factor” curve for each material. Since the powder mass and volume are known in the micro-feeder system, in this work, we characterized an observed density variation during processing via a “displacement-feed factor” profile for each of the fed powders. This curve can be later used for calibrating the system to ensure an accurate, constant feed rate and in addition predicting feeding performance for that material at any feed rate. There is a relation between powder properties and feeding performance. Powders with finer particles and higher compressibility show densification during their feeding process. However, powders with larger particles and lower compressibility show both “densification” and “powder bed expansion,” which is the manifestation of dilation and elastic recovery of particles during the micro-feeding process. Through the application of the displacement-feed factor, it is possible to provide precise feeding accuracy of low-dose materials.

Abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Food intake is usually addressed in pharmacotherapy as a dosing condition or a source of food–drug interactions, yet this view treats food largely as a passive background exposure. To address the separation between therapeutic nutrition and food–drug interaction management, this narrative review proposes a clinically applicable role-based framework that classifies food as a therapeutic agent, an antagonist of pharmacotherapy, or an enabler of treatment according to the dietary exposure, drug and formulation, disease state, timing, and clinical intent. In this framework, food may function as a therapeutic agent, an antagonist of pharmacotherapy, or an enabler of treatment, depending not on the food itself but on the clinical context in which it is consumed. Therapeutic roles include dietary patterns, medically tailored meals, nutrients, and food-derived bioactive compounds that support disease control, symptom relief, nutritional rehabilitation, or treatment responsiveness. Antagonistic roles occur when food reduces efficacy, increases toxicity, or destabilizes response through altered absorption, metabolism, transport, pharmacodynamics, adherence, or food-access constraints. Enabling roles occur when meal timing, composition, or nutritional support increases or stabilizes drug exposure (exposure enablement), reduces gastrointestinal or other treatment-related adverse effects (tolerability enablement), or improves adherence and dosing feasibility (adherence/feasibility enablement). Mechanisms include gastrointestinal physiology, formulation behavior, enzyme and transporter activity, nutrient–drug pharmacodynamics, microbiome effects, and artificial nutrition. Applying this framework requires structured dietary assessment, explicit prescribing instructions, diet-sensitive medication review, and interprofessional care. By classifying food roles conditionally rather than assigning fixed properties to foods, this framework can support more precise prescribing, safer food–drug management, food/formulation design, and patient-centered care.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

Most relevant evidence (with ids):

## pqac-00000005

From text 'archary2016massflowand pages 13-16'.

Hamresin Archary, Walter Schmitz, and Louis Jestin. Mass flow and particle size monitoring of pulverised fuel vertical spindle mills. Chemical and Process Engineering, 37:175-197, Jun 2016. URL: https://doi.org/10.1515/cpe-2016-0016, doi:10.1515/cpe-2016-0016. This article has 10 citations.

This excerpt describes direct optical particle-size measurement, not a predictive model based on feeder or mill operating variables. The PSA uses fibre-optic spatial-filtering velocimetry (SFV) combined with fibre-optic spot scanning (FSS). As a particle crosses an optical fibre, its projected shadow generates an impulse; the measured chord length depends on particle size, particle velocity, and particle/fibre position. A statistical evaluation of many individual particles is required to obtain a representative particle-size distribution, and Bayes’ theorem is noted as a possible method for converting chord-length measurements into particle-size analysis. Reported fineness outputs are mass percentages below 300, 150, 106, and 75 µm; the stated optimal window is 99.00–99.80%, 89.00–94.50%, 76.00–86.50%, and 65.00–75.00%, respectively. Validation consisted of four repeated 15-minute PSA tests and comparison with simultaneous iso-kinetic sampling and sieving. PSA repeatability was reported, with maximum differences of 0.19, 0.67, 2.17, and 2.24 percentage points at those size thresholds. PSA trends agreed with iso-kinetic results, but absolute values differed substantially. The excerpt provides no evidence that feeder speed, feed factor, mass flow, pressure drop, power, air flow, classifier speed, or feeder gravimetric mass time series alone predicts particle size.


---

## pqac-00000006

From text 'archary2016massflowand pages 16-20'.

Hamresin Archary, Walter Schmitz, and Louis Jestin. Mass flow and particle size monitoring of pulverised fuel vertical spindle mills. Chemical and Process Engineering, 37:175-197, Jun 2016. URL: https://doi.org/10.1515/cpe-2016-0016, doi:10.1515/cpe-2016-0016. This article has 10 citations.

The excerpt indicates that particle fineness is inferred using a laser-based Particle Size Analyzer (PSA) probe inserted into the pulverised-fuel pipe. The probe directly measures the chord lengths of particles passing through its laser, rather than deriving size from feeder speed, feed factor, mill mass flow, pressure drop, mill power, air flow, or classifier speed. Reported fineness is expressed as cumulative percentages below four sieve-equivalent sizes: 300, 150, 106, and 75 µm. The PSA measurements are validated by comparison with iso-kinetic sampling results from mills 2B and 2D. That comparison reveals substantial discrepancies: depending on mill and size, PSA readings can indicate finer or coarser material, with the largest cited difference being 123% of the fineness window at 300 µm. The instrument is described as having good repeatability but poor absolute prediction, i.e. high precision and low accuracy under the tested conditions. The investigation attributes deviations to measurement conditions, especially probe angle and purge-air pressure, mass flow, and duration; these parameters can deflect particles and materially change reported fineness. This excerpt contains no evidence that feeder gravimetric mass time series alone predict particle size, and it does not describe a predictive model using the listed mill operating inputs.


---

## pqac-00000007

From text 'archary2016massflowand pages 9-13'.

Hamresin Archary, Walter Schmitz, and Louis Jestin. Mass flow and particle size monitoring of pulverised fuel vertical spindle mills. Chemical and Process Engineering, 37:175-197, Jun 2016. URL: https://doi.org/10.1515/cpe-2016-0016, doi:10.1515/cpe-2016-0016. This article has 10 citations.

This excerpt describes particle-size/fineness measurement as a direct laser-probe measurement in the pulverised-fuel pipe, not as an inference from feeder data. The probe’s laser measures particles passing through a groove, while purge air protects the optics. Five operator-controlled parameters affect the reported fineness: probe rotation/orientation, purge-air pressure, purge-air flow rate, purge duration, and probe depth in the pipe. The excerpt does not identify feeder speed, feed factor, coal mass flow, mill pressure drop, mill power, air flow, classifier speed, or a predictive model using those variables as inputs to calculate particle size. It also does not specify the numerical size outputs or their validation results. For reference, the established validation/comparison method is iso-kinetic PF sampling followed by cyclone separation, laboratory drying, weighing, and sieving to obtain a particle-size distribution. However, this conventional method is labor-intensive, performed only about twice yearly per mill or when a problem is suspected, and is therefore unsuitable for frequent condition monitoring. Nothing in the supplied pages demonstrates that a gravimetric-feeder mass-flow time series alone predicts particle size; the excerpt instead emphasizes that measured fineness depends on the laser probe and its operating configuration.


---

## pqac-00000008

From text 'archary2016massflowand pages 20-22'.

Hamresin Archary, Walter Schmitz, and Louis Jestin. Mass flow and particle size monitoring of pulverised fuel vertical spindle mills. Chemical and Process Engineering, 37:175-197, Jun 2016. URL: https://doi.org/10.1515/cpe-2016-0016, doi:10.1515/cpe-2016-0016. This article has 10 citations.

This excerpt indicates that particle size/fineness is inferred primarily through an online particle size analyser (PSA) probe installed in a pulverised-fuel pipe, rather than from feeder speed or mass-flow data alone. The PSA reports size-fraction results, including the percentages below 300, 150, 106, and 75 micrometres. Its readings depend on practical measurement parameters such as purge-air pressure, flow rate, purge duration, probe angle, and probe penetration depth; these affect particle entrainment and can produce non-representative results. Depth tests showed increasingly coarse readings toward the pipe centre, implying finer particles near the walls, so a single point cannot automatically represent the whole flow. Validation is discussed against iso-kinetic sampling, which traverses nearly the entire pipe cross-section; representative PSA results require traversing and comparison under stable-load conditions. The excerpt separately states that the mill energy-balance model predicts coal mass flow using mill operating information, with an average steady-state error of 2.33%, but it does not specify the complete model inputs here. It also does not provide evidence that feeder-speed or gravimetric mass-flow time series alone predict particle size. Thus, the cited passage supports direct laser-based particle measurement and cross-validation against iso-kinetic sampling, but not a mass-flow-only particle-size model or the full list of requested sensor inputs.

## pqac-00000009

From text 'archary2016massflowand pages 1-3'.

Hamresin Archary, Walter Schmitz, and Louis Jestin. Mass flow and particle size monitoring of pulverised fuel vertical spindle mills. Chemical and Process Engineering, 37:175-197, Jun 2016. URL: https://doi.org/10.1515/cpe-2016-0016, doi:10.1515/cpe-2016-0016. This article has 10 citations.

The excerpt does not provide the detailed particle-size model, sensor-input list, size outputs, or validation results requested; those details presumably occur later in the article. It does establish that particle fineness was intended to be measured directly with a laser-based, on-line particle size analyser, rather than inferred from feeder speed, mill pressure drop, power, air flow, classifier speed, or mass-flow data. The analyser was tested in a power-plant environment and reportedly showed good precision and repeatability, but installation and operating factors affected the perceived results and had to be controlled or accounted for before commissioning. Separately, the paper’s mill-energy-balance method estimates coal mass flow from on-line input data and compares it with a calibrated feeder. The feeder signal is based on screw rotational speed multiplied by a calibration-derived feed factor; because this is a volumetric measurement, it does not automatically account for coal-moisture or density changes. The excerpt therefore gives no support for the claim that a feeder gravimetric mass time series alone predicts particle size. It also does not specify the analyser’s particle-size distribution output, exact model inputs, or the quantitative fineness validation.

## pqac-00000010

From text 'archary2016massflowand pages 22-23'.

Hamresin Archary, Walter Schmitz, and Louis Jestin. Mass flow and particle size monitoring of pulverised fuel vertical spindle mills. Chemical and Process Engineering, 37:175-197, Jun 2016. URL: https://doi.org/10.1515/cpe-2016-0016, doi:10.1515/cpe-2016-0016. This article has 10 citations.

This excerpt does not provide the detailed particle-fineness inference method requested. It states only that the study combines a mill energy-balance model with a particle size analyser (PSA): the model supplies or supports measurement of coal mass flow, while the PSA provides an instantaneous, on-line, real-time particle-size result. It contrasts PSA with isokinetic sampling, noting that isokinetic measurements can be affected by human error through under-sampling or over-sampling, whereas PSA largely removes that source of error. The passage identifies coal mass flow as the quantity parameter and PF particle fineness as the quality parameter, and presents their simultaneous on-line monitoring as the basis for mill condition monitoring and condition-based maintenance. It also cautions that uncertainties in PSA setup and commissioning must be mitigated. However, the excerpt does not specify which operational inputs are used to infer fineness (such as feeder speed, feed factor, pressure drop, mill power, air flow, classifier speed, or mass-flow time series), does not state the size-distribution outputs or size classes, gives no validation results, and does not address whether feeder gravimetric mass alone predicts particle size.

## pqac-00000011

From text 'archary2016massflowand pages 3-6'.

Hamresin Archary, Walter Schmitz, and Louis Jestin. Mass flow and particle size monitoring of pulverised fuel vertical spindle mills. Chemical and Process Engineering, 37:175-197, Jun 2016. URL: https://doi.org/10.1515/cpe-2016-0016, doi:10.1515/cpe-2016-0016. This article has 10 citations.

This excerpt provides background on why particle-size/fineness inference was needed, but it does not contain the later sections that specify the paper’s exact fineness estimator, sensor inputs, output size metrics, or validation results. It states that real-time pulverised-fuel mass flow and particle-size measurement were historically unavailable because of the harsh, abrasive outlet flow. Earlier mill-monitoring approaches used energy-balance models and observer systems, with variables such as mill outlet temperature, pressure drop, coal moisture, and internal unmeasurable coal inventories. The cited multi-segment model represented the mass of coal in the mill, pulverised coal in the mill, and pulverised-coal outlet mass flow as internal variables. The excerpt also notes that some models assumed feeder-reported coal flow was accurate, which may be reasonable for gravimetric feeders but not necessarily for volumetric feeders. Although the passage introduces the authors’ energy-balance model, it ends immediately after the general balance equation and therefore does not establish whether feeder speed, feed factor, mass flow, pressure drop, mill power, air flow, classifier speed, or direct particle measurement are used to infer fineness. It likewise does not state the particle-size outputs, validation procedure, or whether a feeder gravimetric mass time series alone predicts particle size.

## pqac-00000012

From text 'archary2016massflowand pages 6-9'.

Hamresin Archary, Walter Schmitz, and Louis Jestin. Mass flow and particle size monitoring of pulverised fuel vertical spindle mills. Chemical and Process Engineering, 37:175-197, Jun 2016. URL: https://doi.org/10.1515/cpe-2016-0016, doi:10.1515/cpe-2016-0016. This article has 10 citations.

This excerpt describes the mill energy-balance (MEB) model for estimating coal mass flow, not the article’s particle-size/fineness inference method. The model uses an energy balance at steady state: primary-air and seal-air enthalpy, coal energy and moisture, motor power, latent heat for evaporating coal moisture, and convective heat loss. It assumes approximately constant pressure through the heat-transfer region and constant specific heats. Listed fixed inputs include raw-coal temperature, seal-air mass flow, primary-air and seal-air moisture, and convective heat loss. The excerpt notes that mill differential pressure is about 4 kPa, with most pressure drop across the throat and classifier, but it does not identify pressure drop as a direct fineness sensor. The MEB coal-flow estimate was compared with calibrated feeder measurements from five operating mills: the mean difference was 2.33%, while calculated overall uncertainty was 5.13%. Primary-air mass flow contributed the largest individual uncertainty (4.3%), and primary-air temperature, primary-air flow, and mill outlet temperature had the greatest sensitivity. These pages provide no particle-size outputs, classifier-speed model, actual particle-size measurement, fineness validation, or evidence that a feeder gravimetric mass time series alone predicts particle size.

Abstract:
<jats:p>This study presents a comprehensive investigation of turbidity monitoring using two different types of polymer optical fiber (POF) sensors: the reflection–refraction type (RR-POF) and the gap type (Gap-POF). Both sensors were used to visualize and monitor the turbidity changes in suspensions with varying concentrations and different particle compositions, namely silica powder and clay particles. The experiments were conducted by introducing silica powder and clay into water at various concentrations, and the resulting turbidity was measured using both types of POF sensors. The results revealed a significant correlation between particle concentration and light intensity for both kinds of POF sensors. As the particle concentration increased, the light intensity decreased due to increased scattering and absorption effects. For both silica powder and clay suspensions, the light intensity stabilized at lower values as the concentration increased, with the Gap-POF sensor exhibiting higher sensitivity to turbidity changes, particularly at high particle concentrations. Additionally, the study found that the particle composition influenced the sensor response. Silica powder particles caused more irregular fluctuations in light intensity at higher concentrations due to their larger particle size and tendency to aggregate, while clay particles, due to their smaller size and better dispersion, resulted in more stable and gradual changes in light intensity. This highlighted the differences in optical responses between different particle types. Furthermore, the multi-wavelength measurements showed consistent results, with white and green lights exhibiting the strongest response to turbidity changes, while red and blue lights were less sensitive. This wavelength-dependent response was attributed to the scattering and absorption properties of the particles in the suspensions. Both RR-POF and Gap-POF sensors proved to be effective for turbidity monitoring, with Gap-POF demonstrating superior performance in high-concentration suspensions. The findings suggest that POF sensors, particularly Gap-POF, are highly suitable for real-time turbidity monitoring in various particle suspension systems.</jats:p>

Abstract:
The particle size composition of grinding products will significantly affect the technical and economic indexes of subsequent separation operations. The polymetallic complex ores from Tongkeng and Gaofeng are selected as the research object in this paper. Through the JK drop-weight test, the batch grinding test, and the population-balance kinetic model of grinding with the Simulink platform, the grinding characteristics of the two types of ores and the particle-size-composition prediction methods of grinding products are studied. The results show that the impact-crushing capacity of Tongkeng ore and Gaofeng ore are “medium” grade and “soft” grade, respectively. The crushing resistance of Tongkeng ore increases with the decrease in particle size, and the crushing effect is more easily affected by particle size than that of Gaofeng ore. For the same ore, the accuracy order of the three methods is: PSO–BP method > JK drop-weight method > BIII method. For the same method, only the BIII method has higher accuracy in predicting Gaofeng ore than Tongkeng ore, and other methods have better accuracy in predicting Tongkeng ore than Gaofeng ore. The prediction accuracy of the BIII method is inferior to that of the JK drop-weight method and the PSO–BP method and is easily affected by the difference in mineral properties. The PSO–BP method has a high prediction accuracy and fast model operation speed, but the accuracy and speed of the iterative results are easily affected by parameters such as algorithm program weight and threshold. The parameter-solving process of each prediction method is based on different simplifications and assumptions. Therefore, appropriate hypothetical theoretical models should be selected according to different ore properties for practical application.

Abstract:
The optimal utilization of forages is crucial in cattle production, especially in organic dairy systems that encourage forage-based feeding with limited concentrate amounts. Reduction of the particle size of forages is known to improve feed intake and thus might be a viable option to help cows cope with less nutrient-dense feeds. The main aim of this study was to evaluate the effects of reducing forage particle size with a geometric mean of 52 mm (conventional particle size; CON) to 7 mm (reduced particle size; RED) in a high-forage diet (80% of dry matter) on dairy cows' sorting behavior, feed intake, chewing activity, and performance as well as on total-tract nutrient digestibility. Both diets (CON and RED) consisted of 43% grass hay, 37% clover-grass silage, and 20% concentrate and contained roughly 44% NDF, 15% CP, and 0.5% starch (dry matter basis). For CON, particle size was set by mixing all components for 20 min in a vertical feed mixer. The RED diet was treated the same, but before the mixer was filled, forages were chopped (theoretical length of cut = 0.5 cm) and the hay was hammer-milled (sieve size = 2 cm). Four primiparous and 16 multiparous mid-lactating dairy cows were assigned according to milk yield, body weight (BW), days in milk, and parity into 2 groups and fed 1 of the 2 diets for 34 d. The first 13 d were used for diet adaption, followed by data collection of nutrient intake, chewing activity, sorting behavior, milk production, and nutrient digestibility for the last 21 d of the experiment. Seven days before the start of the experiment, data on BW, dry matter intake (DMI), chewing activity, sorting behavior, and milk production were collected for use as covariates. Results showed that the RED diet improved DMI (+1.8 kg/d) and NDF intake (+0.46 kg/d) but decreased intake of physically effective NDF >8 (-3.25 kg/d). The RED-fed cows increased their intake of smaller particles (<19 mm), whereas CON-fed cows sorted for long particles (>19 mm). The RED cows reduced eating and ruminating time per kilogram of DMI by 4.8 and 1.9 min, respectively, suggesting lower mastication efforts. In addition, the RED diet significantly increased apparent total-tract digestibility of nutrients. As a consequence, RED cows' energy-corrected milk yield was higher (27.0 vs. 29.3 kg/d) without affecting milk solids, cow BW, or feed efficiency. In conclusion, the data support a reduction of forage particle size in high-forage diets as a measure to improve energy intake, performance, and hence forage utilization under these feeding conditions.

Abstract:
Simple Summary The poultry meat industry is an important producer of high-quality protein. Broilers require well-balanced and processed diets, which should be environmentally friendly and produced in a sustainable way. The current study was designed to explore opportunities in the feed processing line; it aimed to improve resource savings and broiler performance by changing the particle size of the major ingredients in the diet using hammer or roller mills, and then, pelleting the compound diet using two different conditionings, with an expander or without, prior to pelleting. The hypothesis was that broilers perform better when fed diets processed using a combination of grinding the coarse particles with a roller mill and expanding them before pelleting. The results show that the processing line promotes intense secondary grinding, reducing the particle size. The use of a roller mill, coarse particles and an expander resulted in increased energy utilization, nutrient digestibility and feed conversion ratio of the broiler chickens. Abstract During the processing of compound feed for broilers, several changes occur that affect the physical and probably the nutritional properties of pellets, influencing animal performance. The effects of mill type, particle size (PS) and expander conditioning prior to pelleting (E + P) were combined to generate pellets. A 2 × 3 × 2 factorial arrangement was designed with two mill types (a hammer mill (HM) or roller mill (RM)), three PSs (0.8, 1.2 or 1.6 mm) and two E + Ps (with or without expander processing prior to pelleting), with six replications of 12 unsexed Ross 308 broilers each. All the processing lines reduced the PS from mash to finished pellets via secondary grinding, by 2.35 times on average. However, RM grinding required less electric power (p < 0.001). The intended PS (0.8, 1.2 or 1.6 mm) did not affect this energy consumption. E + P and the PS interacted for the pellet durability index (PDI) (p = 0.006). The worst PDI in the pellets was observed when a PS of 1.6 mm without E + P was used. Only E + P positively affected starch (p < 0.001) and amino acids’ ileal apparent digestibility (p < 0.01). Organic matter (OM) (p = 0.02) and fat (p < 0.001) digestibility, as well as AMEN (p = 0.005) content, were influenced by the PS (main effect), whereas E + P and mill type interacted with these values (p < 0.005). Lower OM digestibility and AMEN content were observed when RM without E + P was used (p = 0.001). The feed conversion ratio (FCR) was enhanced and feed intake (FI) was improved with E + P. The combination of the RM mill, a 1.6 mm mean PS, and E + P improved FCR (three-way interaction, p = 0.019)), showing that for a higher PS, E + P is necessary for animal performance. Carcass yield was, on average, 80.1%. No effects on commercial cuts (breast, legs and wings) were observed. In contrast, abdominal fat was affected by mill type * PS (p = 0.012) and E + P * PS (p = 0.048) in a two-way interaction. The highest abdominal fat indicated an imbalance in the amino acid (AA)-to-AMEN ratio. Coarse PS promoted heavier gizzards (p = 0.02) but E + P tended to reduce them (p = 0.057). The processing steps improved pellet quality and feed efficiency associated with RM, coarse PS and E + P, highlighting the positive effects of E + P on abdominal fat and AMEN content, which should be adjusted to AA or reduced at formulation. However, these results are for an experimental processing plant and may not necessarily apply to larger plants, so the use of these data and methods should be considered as guidelines for replication at production sites.

Abstract:
Particle size distribution is an important parameter of metallurgical coke for use in blast furnaces. It is usually analyzed by traditional sieving methods, which cause delays and require maintenance. In this paper, a coke particle detection model was developed using a deep learning-based object detection algorithm (YOLOv3). The results were used to estimate the particle size distribution by a statistical method. Images of coke on the main conveyor belt of a blast furnace were acquired for model training and testing, and the particle size distribution determined by sieving was used for verification of the results. The experiment results show that the particle detection model is fast and has a high accuracy; the absolute error of the particle size distribution between the detection method and the sieving method was less than 5%. The detection method provides a new approach for fast analysis of particle size distributions from images and holds promise for a future online application in the plant.

Abstract:
Due to the rapid development of electronic devices and their shortened lifespans, waste electrical and electronic equipment (WEEE), or E-waste, is regarded as one of the most fast-growing wastes. Among the categories of E-waste, waste printed circuit boards (WPCBs) are considered the most complex waste materials, owing to their various constitutes, such as plastics, capacitors, wiring, and metal plating. To date, a variety of processing technologies have been developed and studied. However, due to the heterogeneous nature of WPCBs, a thorough study on both material characterization and physical separation was needed to provide a better understanding in material handling, as well as to prepare a suitable feedstock prior to the downstream chemical process. In the present study, integrated size and density separations were performed to understand the liberation of contained metals, particularly Cu and Au, from the plastic substrates. The separation performance was evaluated by the elemental concentration, distribution, and enrichment ratio of valuable metals in different size and density fractions. Further, SEM-EDS on the density separation products was carried out to characterize the surface morphology, elemental mapping, and quantified elemental contents. Moreover, thermo-gravimetric properties of waste PCBs were investigated by TGA, in order to understand the effect of temperature on volatile and combustible fractions during the thermal processing.

Abstract:
Diesel exhaust particles (DEPs) can deposit onto the respiratory epithelial surface upon inhalation. The quantification of DEP deposition on cells is important for understanding dose–response relationships within tissues. However, continuous, nondestructive methods for monitoring DEP deposition on cells remain challenging. We investigated a miniaturized thermosensitive detection system (CalorQuanti) and integrated it into the VITROCELL Cloud Alpha system, the so-called Cloud Alpha/CalorQuanti, to combine cell exposure to particles at the air–liquid interface (ALI) and online particle monitoring on cells. The Cloud Alpha/CalorQuanti demonstrates uniform particle deposition, providing the basis for online monitoring of particles on cells. With low detection limits (93 to 415 ng/cm2) for gold nanoparticles (AuNPs, as test material) and DEPs, the device showed strong positive relationships (R 2 ≥ 0.95) between particle concentrations measured and thermal signal intensities generated on cells under dry and humid conditions. It also possesses the versatility to optimize online particle detection on cells by adjusting measurement parameters to balance sensitivity and phototoxicity. The Cloud Alpha/CalorQuanti allows exposure to aerosolized DEPs at ALI while providing sensitive monitoring and quantification of DEP deposition on cells. This device is useful for monitoring combustion-derived carbon-based particle exposure on cells following laboratory simulation and field exposures, advancing environmental health research.

Sara Fathollahi, Pauline H. M. Janssen, Bram Bekaert, Dirk Vanderroost, Valerie Vanhoorne, and Bastiaan H. J. Dickhoff. Understanding powder behavior in continuous feeding: powder densification and screw layering. Powders, 3:482-499, Sep 2024. URL: https://doi.org/10.3390/powders3040026, doi:10.3390/powders3040026. This article has 5 citations.

For the 2024 densification study, particle-size distribution was measured separately from feeder experiments using dry laser diffraction, with three measurements per material. Bulk and tapped densities were also measured independently, and the Hausner ratio was calculated as tapped density divided by bulk density. Feeding was performed with a loss-in-weight twin-screw feeder at a total system flow rate of 20 kg/h; feeder data were collected at 1 Hz, including net weight, screw speed, mass flow rate, feed factor, and feeding mode. The excerpt does not specifically discuss Yang and Evans (2007) or Hou (2024), nor does it establish a particle-size-dependent dosing law or show that particle size/PSD can be estimated as an output from gravimetric mass-time traces. It does, however, provide relevant constraints for interpreting dosing performance. Powder cohesion and aggregation produce flow-rate fluctuations even when the mean rate is constant, while changes in bulk density can decouple volumetric delivery from mass feedrate. Density varies with consolidation, moisture, particle size, segregation, and attrition; therefore, volumetric feeding requires density stability, whereas gravimetric/loss-in-weight control compensates for density changes by feedback. Feeder performance also depends on the selected hopper, flow aids, weighing platform, and dispensing mechanism, with screw, vibration, belt, and rotary-valve mechanisms identified. In loss-in-weight operation, the hopper and feeder are weighed over time; the controller calculates feedrate from the change in measured mass divided by time and adjusts the dispensing mechanism toward the setpoint. Thus, mass-time traces directly support feedrate estimation and control, but the excerpt gives no basis for uniquely inferring particle size or PSD from those traces. Such inference would require an independently validated relationship separating particle-size effects from density, moisture, cohesion, consolidation, geometry, and feedback dynamics.

The excerpt describes two distinct measurement applications, but it does not report a study of segregation using automated gravimetric powder dispensing, nor does it identify Wu, Desai et al. (2021). In the micro-dosing experiments, a Sartorius analytical scale functioned as a catch scale to measure the total mass delivered by a single-screw feeder. The camera-based system estimated delivered mass indirectly from image brightness after calibration against the scale, and accuracy was assessed by comparing target or catch-scale weights with videometric estimates using RMSEP and TOST analysis. Thus, this is a gravimetric assay of total delivered mass, not a direct measurement of particle-size distribution or size fraction in the dispensed material. Separately, the excerpt reports validation of a camera-based particle-size measurement system using MCC pellets, with comparisons against spatial filtering velocimetry and laser diffraction. That PSD work concerns particle sizing and method comparison, but it is not linked here to automated gravimetric dispensing or segregation evaluation. Consequently, the excerpt supports distinguishing mass-flow/dose verification from direct PSD or size-fraction measurement, but provides no evidence that gravimetric dispensing was used to evaluate segregation by measuring delivered PSD.

## pqac-00000036

J. Torres-Serra, A. Rodríguez-Ferran, and E. Romero. Classification of granular materials via flowability-based clustering with application to bulk feeding. Powder Technology, 378:288-302, Jan 2021. URL: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.powtec.2020.09.022, doi:10.1016/j.powtec.2020.09.022. This article has 14 citations and is from a domain leading peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt indicates that the model input features comprise two groups: conventional material properties and specialised flow/kinematic descriptors. DS2 uses 8 conventional properties, including bulk density, Hausner ratio, median particle size d50, gradation coefficients Cu and Cc, water content, particle density, and friction coefficient, plus 118 specialised variables. The specialised variables are derived from the granular-flow experiment, including basal load profiles and velocity/kinematic quantities obtained with beam load cells and high-speed video/PIV. The analysis uses PCA and flowability-based similarity/clustering of observations; this passage does not identify a separate supervised target label, so cluster membership or flowability similarity appears to be the analytical outcome rather than a directly stated label. Particle size and PSD descriptors are represented as measured conventional predictors: d50, Cu, and Cc come from sieving analysis, while density and friction are measured or taken from specified sources. Nothing here indicates that particle size or PSD is predicted directly from gravimetric mass-time traces or mass-flow fluctuations alone. Training/analysis data are generated using the granular flow test setup, load cells, high-speed imaging/PIV, and separate material-characterisation procedures such as sieving, water-content measurement, fluid-displacement density measurement, and friction data.

URL: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.powtec.2020.09.022, doi:10.1016/j.powtec.2020.09.022. This article has 14 citations and is from a domain leading peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt describes a material-characterisation and clustering model, not a model that predicts particle size or PSD from gravimetric feeder mass-time signals. The apparent input/features are six measured granular-material variables: HR (Hausner ratio), θ (angle of repose), ρb (bulk density), d50 (median particle size), Cu (uniformity coefficient), and Cc (coefficient of curvature). PCA reduces these measurements to projected variables, with the first three used for visualisation and clustering. Thus d50 and the PSD descriptors Cu and Cc are themselves measured explanatory variables/features; they are not outputs predicted from feeding traces in the described analysis. The labels or comparison classes are feeder-system types: fluidisation chamber, gravity, screw, screw with deaeration, and belt. K-means is initialized using feeder-type centroids and then produces five flowability-based clusters, which are compared with those feeder labels. This excerpt does not identify the instruments used to measure HR, angle of repose, bulk density, d50, Cu, or Cc, nor does it describe training data generated from mass-time traces or mass-flow fluctuations. Consequently, claims about specific instruments or trace-based prediction would require other sections of the paper; the provided pages only establish that the particle/flow properties were measured separately and used as clustering variables.

 1   Abstract


 2    In this study, the volumetric and gravimetric feeding behavior of 15 pharmaceutical

 3   powders on a low feed rate feeder was correlated with their material properties through a

 4    multivariate approach. The powders under investigation differ substantially in terms of

 5   material properties, making the selected powders representative for powders typically

 6   used in pharmaceutical manufacturing. The material properties were described by 25

 7   material property descriptors, obtained from a rational selection of critical characterization

 8   techniques that provided maximal information with minimal characterization effort. From

 9   volumetric feeding experiments  (i.e., powder feed rate not controlled), the maximum

10   feeding capacity (maximum feed factor (FFmax)) and optimal hopper fill level at which the

11   feeder should be refilled during gravimetric feeding (feed factor decay (FFdecay)) were

12   obtained. During gravimetric feeding experiments (i.e., powder feed rate controlled), the

13    variability on the feed rate (relative standard deviation (RSD)) and the difference between

14   the setpoint and mean feed rate (relative error (RE)) were determined. Partial least

15   squares (PLS) regression was applied to correlate the volumetric and gravimetric feeding

16   responses (Y) with the material property descriptors (X). The predictive ability of the

17   developed PLS models was assessed by predicting the feeding responses of two new

18   powders  (i.e., validation set). Overall, the volumetric feeding responses (FFmax and

19    FFdecay) were predicted better than the gravimetric feeding responses (RSD and RE),

20   since in gravimetric mode the impact of material properties on the feeding behavior is

21   reduced due to the control system of the feeder. Especially RE was weakly correlated with

22   material properties as RE of most powders varied around zero with only a small numerical

23    variation. Interestingly, this confirms that the control system is working properly and that                                                                                 3


24   the feeder is capable of feeding different powders accurately at low feed rates. The

25   developed models allowed to predict the feeding behavior of new powders based on their

26   material properties. Consequently the number of feeding experiments during process

27   development can be greatly reduced, thereby leading to a more efficient and faster

28   development of new drug products.

45   1. INTRODUCTION


46    In a continuous manufacturing line, feeding of the raw materials is generally the first unit

47   operation and is crucial towards the success of the complete manufacturing process

48   (Simonaho et al., 2016). Inaccurate and inconsistent feeding of raw materials can lead to

49   an impaired product  quality  (e.g.,  incorrect  active pharmaceutical ingredient (API)

50   concentration), since the composition of the final product is determined by the feed rate

51    of the individual raw materials (Ervasti et al., 2015). Loss-in-weight (LIW) feeders consist

52    of a feeding device, weighing platform and control system (Engisch and Muzzio, 2015a).

53   The feeding device is placed on the weighing platform, which measures the weight of the

54   feeding device together with the powder in the feeding device. A LIW feeder can work in

55   two modes,  i.e., gravimetric or volumetric. In gravimetric mode, the control system

56   acquires the mass of the feeding device and its content from the weighing platform as a

57   function of time during feeding. The actual feed rate is calculated from the difference in

58   mass, measured by the weighing platform, divided by the difference in time between

59   consecutive measurements. The control system minimizes the difference between the

60   actual feed rate and the feed rate setpoint by adjusting the dispensing rate (e.g., screw

61   speed) of the feeding device (Coperion K-Tron, 2012). Thus in gravimetric mode the

62   powder feed rate is controlled to account for sources of variability, such as variations in

63   material density when the powder level in the hopper changes during feeding (Van Snick

64    et al., 2017a). The volumetric mode is characterized by the displacement of a constant

65   material volume per unit of time instead of a constant mass per unit of time as in

66   gravimetric mode. The screw speed of the feeding device  is kept constant during

67   volumetric feeding, implying that the powder feed rate is not controlled (Blackshields and                                                                                 5


68   Crean, 2017). For pharmaceutical applications, where the feeding accuracy of the

69    individual raw materials is critical and the density of the processed powders can vary, the

70   gravimetric feeding mode is preferred. A LIW feed

Kobayashi et al. measure particle-size-distribution descriptors D10, D50, and D90, defined as the particle diameters below which 10%, 50%, and 90% of particles fall, respectively. However, these PSD descriptors are material-property measurements used as inputs or characterization variables; the prediction target is not PSD. The modeled quantity is the feed factor, f, calculated as instantaneous flow rate F divided by screw rotation speed ω (equivalently, mass per revolution). The models therefore predict the feed-factor value/profile as a function of hopper powder weight and other experimental/material variables, rather than predicting D10, D50, or D90 from mass per revolution. The candidate input-variable groups include powder weight in the hopper (W), screw rotation speed (ω), ethenzamide mass fraction (XAPI), and measured material properties (Props). The material properties include PSD descriptors among other powder properties, so PSD can inform feed-factor prediction when included in a variable group, but the study does not establish that feed factor or mass per revolution predicts PSD. The physical model specifically describes the nonlinear relationship between feed factor and powder weight in the hopper; alternative data-driven and gray-box models incorporate fraction, operating speed, and material-property information.

## pqac-00000056

From text 'yang2007meteringanddispensing pages 9-10'.

URL: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.powtec.2007.04.004, doi:10.1016/j.powtec.2007.04.004. This article has 208 citations and is from a domain leading peer-reviewed journal.

The Yang and Evans review provides limited but relevant support for linking powder-feeding behavior to particle size. It reports that, for narrow particle-size-distribution fractions dispensed through a given tube, dose was inversely proportional to particle size. This is the closest explicit particle-size/feeding-mass relationship in the excerpt and could motivate a powder-specific calibration, but it is not presented as a general quantitative correlation suitable for inferring size from arbitrary feeding traces. The review emphasizes that discharged mass is also governed by vibration amplitude, acceleration, particle kinetic energy, capillary or orifice dimensions, frequency, and wall-friction effects. In ultrasonic capillary feeding, flow rate was highly sensitive to capillary diameter and power, with a vibrating powder layer near the wall acting as a lubricant. The cited ultrasonic systems reached approximately 10 μg/s for powders around 3 μm, while individual tungsten-carbide doses as low as 50 μg were obtained. These observations indicate that distinct fed-mass fluctuations or flow trends may reflect particle size, but they are confounded by apparatus and operating parameters. The excerpt contains no FF metric, no time-resolved fluctuation analysis, and no regression or calibration curve of particle size versus FF. Thus, it offers qualitative mechanistic guidance and one inverse dose-size relationship, rather than validated evidence for a universal PSD-independent particle-size proxy.

## pqac-00000057

From text 'bostijn2019amultivariateapproach pages 22-26'.

N. Bostijn, J. Dhondt, A. Ryckaert, E. Szabó, W. Dhondt, B. V. Snick, B. V. Snick, V. Vanhoorne, C. Vervaet, and T. D. Beer. A multivariate approach to predict the volumetric and gravimetric feeding behavior of a low feed rate feeder based on raw material properties. International Journal of Pharmaceutics, 557:342–353, Feb 2019. URL: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ijpharm.2018.12.066, doi:10.1016/j.ijpharm.2018.12.066. This article has 90 citations and is from a domain leading peer-reviewed journal.

This Bostijn et al. excerpt provides indirect evidence that particle size can influence feeding-trace behavior, but it does not establish a calibrated particle-size proxy from feed-factor (FF) data. In the gravimetric feeding model, powders with small particle size were associated with greater feed-rate variability when combined with low density, poor flow, and high compressibility; the proposed mechanism was inconsistent screw filling. For FFmax, however, density and powder flow were identified as the material properties with the largest impact. The excerpt gives a concrete contrast between lactose (CL) and PH105: despite similar bulk density, CL had higher FFmax, attributed to better flow. FFdecay was primarily associated with compressibility, while flow and density were negatively correlated with FFdecay. No quantitative particle-size-versus-FF correlation, regression coefficient, controlled particle-size-fraction experiment, or distinct FF trend attributable specifically to particle size is reported in these pages. Particle size appears as one descriptor within a multivariate model and is confounded with other powder properties. Thus, this source may support particle size as a potentially relevant covariate for powder-specific modeling of variability, but not as evidence for replacing PSD measurements with a universally calibrated size proxy. Additional studies with experimentally separated size fractions and independently reported FF trajectories would be needed.

Fathollahi et al. provide a qualitative basis for interpreting particle size from powder-feeding traces, but the excerpt does not establish a calibrated, powder-specific particle-size proxy or a quantitative particle-size-versus-feed-fluctuation (FF) correlation. The study compares several materials with substantially different particle-size distributions and reports that larger-particle, lower-compressibility powders initially produce higher feed rates and stronger initial densification, whereas finer, more compressible powders densify only slightly. CapsuLac60 and dicalcium phosphate show a distinctive nonmonotonic trace: feed rate decreases initially to a minimum and then rises, unlike the finer powders. However, feeding behavior is explicitly attributed to multiple coupled properties—particle-size distribution, bulk density, compressibility, and elastic behavior—so particle size cannot be isolated as the causal predictor. The excerpt reports material-level trends rather than experiments in which particle-size fractions were systematically varied within one powder and their fed-mass fluctuations quantified. It also does not provide regression coefficients, sensitivity values, or an FF metric linked independently to particle size. Thus, this paper can support hypothesis generation and qualitative classification of trace shapes, but not a validated size estimator independent of PSD and powder rheology.

This excerpt from Bostijn et al. is relevant for defining and extracting powder-feeding trace features, but it does not provide a direct particle-size calibration. The study tested 15 distinct pharmaceutical raw materials, including dense, powder, and micronized paracetamol/API categories, so these materials may offer qualitative contrasts associated with particle size. However, the excerpt does not state that particle-size fractions of the same material were experimentally prepared or varied systematically; the powders appear to be separate commercial/raw-material identities. Volumetric feeding was conducted at 6, 30, and 54 rpm, with feed rate recorded every second using a catch scale. The resulting feed-factor profile plots feed factor (mass per screw revolution) against hopper fill level. Two extracted descriptors are especially relevant as potential powder-specific trace proxies: FFmax, the maximum observed feed factor and a measure of feeding capacity, and FFdecay, the hopper-fill level at which feed factor falls to 90% of FFmax. The excerpt documents a general decrease in feed factor as hopper fill decreases, but it gives no quantitative correlation between particle size and FFmax, FFdecay, fluctuation magnitude, or another trace statistic. Thus, Bostijn supports a methodology for deriving calibrated, material-specific feeding signatures, but not a validated particle-size proxy independent of PSD. Establishing such a proxy would require within-material size-fraction experiments and reported statistical correlations.

Separately, volumetric feeding responses were characterized as FFmax and FFdecay at screw speeds of 6, 30, and 54 rpm for each powder. The study also measured gravimetric variability and error at 0.1 and 0.55 kg/h, although those metrics are not particle-size correlations in this excerpt. Thus, Bostijn supports pairing an experimentally measured size descriptor such as dv50 with feed-factor responses across powders and screw speeds. However, these pages describe methods only: they do not document experimentally varied particle-size fractions, distinct fed-mass fluctuation patterns attributable specifically to size, regression coefficients, or a calibrated powder-specific size proxy based on FF. Journal of Pharmaceutical Innovation, Feb 2025. URL: https://doi.org/10.1007/s12247-025-09927-0, doi:10.1007/s12247-025-09927-0. This article has 0 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

function.arguments:
{"answer": "## Finding

**I did not find a published, validated demonstration that predicts a powder’s particle size or particle-size distribution (PSD) *from gravimetric feeder or dispenser data alone***—whether balance mass-versus-time readings, fluctuations in the derived mass-flow rate, or mass delivered per screw revolution. This is a qualified literature-search finding, not proof that no such method exists. The closest studies establish that particle size *affects* feeding, or use feeder signals to infer packing and equipment behavior, but they do not report size or PSD as the predicted output. (pqac-00000044, pqac-00000015, pqac-00000045, pqac-00000049)

The distinction between what was measured and what was predicted is central:

<artifact id="artifact-00"/>

**The closest signal-based inference** is Fathollahi and colleagues’ 2024 loss-in-weight study. They logged hopper weight, mass flow, screw speed, and *feed factor*—grams delivered per revolution—at 1 Hz. Changes in the feed-factor profile were interpreted as evidence of powder densification within feeding cycles and powder layering on the screws across cycles. PSD, however, was measured separately by laser diffraction, not reconstructed from that profile. Their Figure 4 illustrates the two feed-factor trends used for those *operational* diagnoses. (pqac-00000045, pqac-00000046, pqac-00000048)

**There is a plausible size signal, but not a demonstrated inverse estimator.** In a micro-feeder study with an outlet balance, finer and more compressible powders generally showed different effective-density and feeding trajectories from coarser powders; the authors used the gravimetric data to characterize density variation and improve feed-rate prediction, not to estimate size. In a lactose-feeding comparison, the finest grade had the lowest feed factor, yet two grades with nearly identical PSDs also fed differently under some configurations. An earlier dispensing review reported an inverse relationship between dose and particle size for *narrow size fractions in a particular tube*, but did not turn that relationship into a general, validated balance-trace-to-PSD method. (pqac-00000014, pqac-00000015, pqac-00000058, pqac-00000061, pqac-00000027)

**Why mass per revolution is not itself a size measurement.** If screw geometry is fixed, mass delivered per revolution reflects how much of its available volume the powder fills *and the density of that filled powder*. Both can change with hopper level, consolidation, flowability, cohesion, adhesion to the screws, and operating conditions. In gravimetric mode, feedback also changes screw speed to hold mass flow near its setpoint, potentially suppressing differences in the flow-rate trace while leaving differences in feed factor. Consequently, different PSDs can plausibly yield similar signals, and similar PSDs can yield different signals; a full PSD is especially difficult to identify uniquely from one aggregate mass measurement. This is an inference from the reported feeder physics and comparisons, not an experimentally proven impossibility. (pqac-00000031, pqac-00000055, pqac-00000046, pqac-00000061)

A **powder- and instrument-specific classifier or estimate of a limited size statistic**, such as a change in median size or fines content, remains a reasonable research hypothesis. Demonstrating it would require independently measured PSD labels for systematically varied size fractions of the *same material*, synchronized balance and screw-speed records, controlled density/moisture/fill-level and operating conditions, and validation on held-out batches. Existing studies provide candidate trace features—feed-factor level and decay, cycle trends, and feed-rate variability—but do **not** establish the accuracy or generalizability of such an inverse model. Where actual online fineness was reported alongside feeder-derived flow information in a pulverized-fuel study, the size measurement came instead from a separate optical particle-size probe. (pqac-00000059, pqac-00000060, pqac-00000046, pqac-00000005, pqac-00000009)"}
