state.question: Has anyone inferred or predicted the particle size or particle size distribution of a powder from gravimetric dispensing or feeding data, that is, from balance mass-versus-time readings, mass-flow-rate fluctuations, or the mass delivered per screw revolution of a screw/auger feeder, loss-in-weight feeder or automated powder dosing instrument?

answer.question: Has anyone inferred or predicted the particle size or particle size distribution of a powder from gravimetric dispensing or feeding data, that is, from balance mass-versus-time readings, mass-flow-rate fluctuations, or the mass delivered per screw revolution of a screw/auger feeder, loss-in-weight feeder or automated powder dosing instrument?
answer.answer:
No. ## Finding

**I did not find a published, validated demonstration that predicts a powder’s particle size or particle-size distribution (PSD) *from gravimetric feeder or dispenser data alone***—whether balance mass-versus-time readings, fluctuations in the derived mass-flow rate, or mass delivered per screw revolution. This is a qualified literature-search finding, not proof that no such method exists. The closest studies establish that particle size *affects* feeding, or use feeder signals to infer packing and equipment behavior, but they do not report size or PSD as the predicted output. (bostijn2019amultivariateapproach pages 1-6, fathollahi2020performanceevaluationof pages 1-2, fathollahi2024understandingpowderbehavior pages 3-5, kobayashi2024feedfactorprofile pages 3-4)

The distinction between what was measured and what was predicted is central:

| Study | Feeder-derived measurement | Actual size-related role / conclusion |
|---|---|---|
| Bostijn et al. (2019) | Feed-factor maximum and decay (`FFmax`, `FFdecay`), plus gravimetric feed-rate variability and relative error (`RSD`, `RE`) | Laser-diffraction `dv50` was an independently measured input used to predict feeder responses—not an output inferred from gravimetry. (bostijn2019amultivariateapproach pages 1-6, bostijn2019amultivariateapproach pages 14-18) |
| Fathollahi et al. (2020) | Catch-balance discharged mass at 1 s intervals and a displacement-feed-factor profile characterizing effective-density changes | Particle size was measured separately by laser diffraction. Trace differences were associated jointly with size, compressibility, packing, and density; PSD was not predicted from the balance trace. (fathollahi2020performanceevaluationof pages 4-5, fathollahi2020performanceevaluationof pages 5-7) |
| Fathollahi et al. (2024) | LIW data at 1 Hz; feed factor in g/rev, with local and overall trends used to indicate densification and screw layering | PSD was measured separately by dry laser diffraction. Feed-factor trends diagnose feeder phenomena, not particle size or PSD. (fathollahi2024understandingpowderbehavior pages 3-5, fathollahi2024understandingpowderbehavior pages 8-10, fathollahi2024understandingpowderbehavior media b6404b79) |
| Kobayashi et al. (2024) | Feed-factor profile—mass delivered per screw rotation as a function of hopper powder weight | Models predict the feed-factor profile from hopper weight, API fraction, screw speed, and optionally independently measured properties including `D10`, `D50`, and `D90`; they do not invert feed factor to obtain PSD. (kobayashi2024feedfactorprofile pages 1-2, kobayashi2024feedfactorprofile pages 3-4, kobayashi2024feedfactorprofile pages 2-3) |
| Jaspers et al. (2025) | Feed factor under different feeder configurations | The finest lactose grade had the lowest feed factor, but grades with nearly identical PSDs behaved differently, showing that size is not uniquely recoverable from feed factor. (jaspers2025optimizingcontinuousfeeding pages 5-8) |
| Archary et al. (2016) | Feeder speed/feed factor supported coal mass-flow estimation | Online PSD/fineness came from a separate laser particle-size probe and was validated against sampling and sieving—not inferred from feeder gravimetry. (archary2016massflowand pages 13-16, archary2016massflowand pages 20-22, archary2016massflowand pages 1-3) |
| **Overall finding** | **Balance mass-time, mass-flow fluctuations, or mass per revolution** | **None of these studies predicts particle size or PSD from feeder gravimetry; size is independently measured, used as an input/covariate, or obtained from a separate optical sensor.** |


*Table: The closest published studies use particle size as an independently measured input or infer feeder phenomena such as density change and screw layering. None of the listed studies reconstructs particle size or PSD from gravimetric feeder data alone.*

**The closest signal-based inference** is Fathollahi and colleagues’ 2024 loss-in-weight study. They logged hopper weight, mass flow, screw speed, and *feed factor*—grams delivered per revolution—at 1 Hz. Changes in the feed-factor profile were interpreted as evidence of powder densification within feeding cycles and powder layering on the screws across cycles. PSD, however, was measured separately by laser diffraction, not reconstructed from that profile. Their Figure 4 illustrates the two feed-factor trends used for those *operational* diagnoses. (fathollahi2024understandingpowderbehavior pages 3-5, fathollahi2024understandingpowderbehavior pages 8-10, fathollahi2024understandingpowderbehavior media b6404b79)

**There is a plausible size signal, but not a demonstrated inverse estimator.** In a micro-feeder study with an outlet balance, finer and more compressible powders generally showed different effective-density and feeding trajectories from coarser powders; the authors used the gravimetric data to characterize density variation and improve feed-rate prediction, not to estimate size. In a lactose-feeding comparison, the finest grade had the lowest feed factor, yet two grades with nearly identical PSDs also fed differently under some configurations. An earlier dispensing review reported an inverse relationship between dose and particle size for *narrow size fractions in a particular tube*, but did not turn that relationship into a general, validated balance-trace-to-PSD method. (fathollahi2020performanceevaluationof pages 4-5, fathollahi2020performanceevaluationof pages 1-2, fathollahi2020performanceevaluationof pages 5-7, jaspers2025optimizingcontinuousfeeding pages 5-8, yang2007meteringanddispensing pages 9-10)

**Why mass per revolution is not itself a size measurement.** If screw geometry is fixed, mass delivered per revolution reflects how much of its available volume the powder fills *and the density of that filled powder*. Both can change with hopper level, consolidation, flowability, cohesion, adhesion to the screws, and operating conditions. In gravimetric mode, feedback also changes screw speed to hold mass flow near its setpoint, potentially suppressing differences in the flow-rate trace while leaving differences in feed factor. Consequently, different PSDs can plausibly yield similar signals, and similar PSDs can yield different signals; a full PSD is especially difficult to identify uniquely from one aggregate mass measurement. This is an inference from the reported feeder physics and comparisons, not an experimentally proven impossibility. (engisch2014lossinweightfeedingin pages 22-27, bostijn2019amultivariateapproach pages 22-26, fathollahi2024understandingpowderbehavior pages 8-10, jaspers2025optimizingcontinuousfeeding pages 5-8)

A **powder- and instrument-specific classifier or estimate of a limited size statistic**, such as a change in median size or fines content, remains a reasonable research hypothesis. Demonstrating it would require independently measured PSD labels for systematically varied size fractions of the *same material*, synchronized balance and screw-speed records, controlled density/moisture/fill-level and operating conditions, and validation on held-out batches. Existing studies provide candidate trace features—feed-factor level and decay, cycle trends, and feed-rate variability—but do **not** establish the accuracy or generalizability of such an inverse model. Where actual online fineness was reported alongside feeder-derived flow information in a pulverized-fuel study, the size measurement came instead from a separate optical particle-size probe. (bostijn2019amultivariateapproach pages 10-14, bostijn2019amultivariateapproach pages 14-18, fathollahi2024understandingpowderbehavior pages 8-10, archary2016massflowand pages 13-16, archary2016massflowand pages 1-3)

contexts.context: The excerpt describes a loss-in-weight feeder whose primary measured signal is total feeder, hopper, and powder weight versus time. The derivative of weight loss provides the fed mass-flow rate, which is compared with a target; the controller adjusts motor/screw speed. During hopper refill, the load cell becomes effectively unavailable, so volumetric control or an inferred feed-factor-based strategy is used. The feed factor is defined as outlet mass flow rate divided by screw velocity (mass per screw revolution), making screw speed the manipulated/input variable and mass flow the controlled/output variable during normal gravimetric operation. The text interprets feed factor as an indirect indicator of powder density: higher mass per revolution implies higher density. Refill can compact the residual powder, increasing density and causing overfeeding, reported as approximately +1% to +10–15% depending on material. The excerpt discusses density, flow properties, hopper level, and feed-rate error, but does not describe particle size or particle-size distribution as an explicitly estimated output from balance weight-time data, feed fluctuations, mass per revolution, or feed factor. It also contains no discussion of Li, Bostijn, Yang, Fathollahi, or Hou, and no inversion from feeder measurements to particle-size output is specified.

contexts.context: This excerpt describes direct optical particle-size measurement, not a predictive model based on feeder or mill operating variables. The PSA uses fibre-optic spatial-filtering velocimetry (SFV) combined with fibre-optic spot scanning (FSS). As a particle crosses an optical fibre, its projected shadow generates an impulse; the measured chord length depends on particle size, particle velocity, and particle/fibre position. A statistical evaluation of many individual particles is required to obtain a representative particle-size distribution, and Bayes’ theorem is noted as a possible method for converting chord-length measurements into particle-size analysis. Reported fineness outputs are mass percentages below 300, 150, 106, and 75 µm; the stated optimal window is 99.00–99.80%, 89.00–94.50%, 76.00–86.50%, and 65.00–75.00%, respectively. Validation consisted of four repeated 15-minute PSA tests and comparison with simultaneous iso-kinetic sampling and sieving. PSA repeatability was reported, with maximum differences of 0.19, 0.67, 2.17, and 2.24 percentage points at those size thresholds. PSA trends agreed with iso-kinetic results, but absolute values differed substantially. The excerpt provides no evidence that feeder speed, feed factor, mass flow, pressure drop, power, air flow, classifier speed, or feeder gravimetric mass time series alone predicts particle size.

contexts.context: The excerpt indicates that particle fineness is inferred using a laser-based Particle Size Analyzer (PSA) probe inserted into the pulverised-fuel pipe. contexts.context: This excerpt describes the mill energy-balance (MEB) model for estimating coal mass flow, not the article’s particle-size/fineness inference method. The model uses an energy balance at steady state: primary-air and seal-air enthalpy, coal energy and moisture, motor power, latent heat for evaporating coal moisture, and convective heat loss. It assumes approximately constant pressure through the heat-transfer region and constant specific heats. Listed fixed inputs include raw-coal temperature, seal-air mass flow, primary-air and seal-air moisture, and convective heat loss. The excerpt notes that mill differential pressure is about 4 kPa, with most pressure drop across the throat and classifier, but it does not identify pressure drop as a direct fineness sensor. The MEB coal-flow estimate was compared with calibrated feeder measurements from five operating mills: the mean difference was 2.33%, while calculated overall uncertainty was 5.13%. Primary-air mass flow contributed the largest individual uncertainty (4.3%), and primary-air temperature, primary-air flow, and mill outlet temperature had the greatest sensitivity. contexts.context: For the 2024 densification study, particle-size distribution was measured separately from feeder experiments using dry laser diffraction, with three measurements per material. Bulk and tapped densities were also measured independently, and the Hausner ratio was calculated as tapped density divided by bulk density. Feeding was performed with a loss-in-weight twin-screw feeder at a total system flow rate of 20 kg/h; feeder data were collected at 1 Hz, including net weight, screw speed, mass flow rate, feed factor, and feeding mode. The feed factor was defined as grams transported per screw revolution and its time profile was used to investigate powder densification and screw-layering behavior. The excerpt does not describe a direct gravimetric measurement of particle displacement, nor does it report predicting particle size as an output. It also provides no quantitative correlations between particle size and feed-factor or density changes in these pages. Important caveats include exclusion of the first 300 seconds to remove screw-priming effects and filtering observations outside ±10% of the mass-flow set point to remove external disturbances. Thus, this excerpt supports separate particle-size characterization and feeder-based monitoring of apparent densification, but not claims about predictive particle-size modeling or quantified cross-property correlations.

contexts.context: This excerpt from Fathollahi et al. (2021) describes a calibration-based control strategy for continuous low-dose feeding. A material-specific factor, described in the excerpt as not being affected by feed rate, was obtained during calibration runs. That factor was then used to predict feed rate and proactively adjust piston displacement speed. The approach specifically addressed changes in effective displacement density during processing, minimizing their impact on feed rate. Stable operation at feed-rate set points was achieved through predefined piston-speed modifications based on the prediction model. The study also combined feed-forward control with iterative learning control and transferred the strategy to a physical micro-feeding system. Di-calcium phosphate was demonstrated at 10 g/h. The excerpt reports that relative deviation from the set point and relative standard deviation decreased significantly, especially for materials showing large uncontrolled feed-rate fluctuations, but it supplies no numerical correlation coefficients, error values, or detailed gravimetric measurement protocol here. contexts.context: The excerpt provides information for Fathollahi et al. (2024), but not the 2020 or 2021 studies. In the 2024 work, gravimetric feeding was evaluated from recorded feeder mass loss and mass flow rate (MF), while feed factor (FF, g/rev) was used to reveal changes that the closed-loop controller compensated for by changing screw speed. MF was held at 18.8 kg/h with RSD values below 1.3%, whereas FF variation (RSD below 2%) indicated slight densification and/or screw layering. Local FF linear-regression slopes were used as an operational measure of densification in the hopper–screw zone; the overall FF regression slope was used as a measure of screw layering across cycles. The excerpt does not report separately measured particle sizes, does not describe particle size as a predicted output, and does not provide quantitative correlations between particle size and densification, layering, or feeding performance. Important caveats are that stronger apparent densification occurred during initial startup cycles because screw filling and the feeder’s initial assumptions were still stabilizing; these startup effects diminished once control was established. The study also cautions that minimal layering for lactose may not generalize to micronized APIs, for which severe layering can eventually require process stoppage and screw cleaning.

contexts.context: For Fathollahi et al. (2020), the excerpt describes a direct gravimetric measurement: discharged material amount was recorded by the balance at 1-second intervals while the scraper operated at 10 rpm, with otherwise constant setup parameters. Particle size was characterized separately using HELOS laser diffraction over 0.45–875 μm, with measurements performed in triplicate; the study used materials spanning substantially different sizes, including CapsuLac60 (d50 = 244 μm), GranuLac200 (31 μm), di-calcium phosphate (184 μm), croscarmellose sodium (43 μm), and silicon dioxide (20 μm). Feeding behavior was interpreted through the relative effective displacement density, ρ*ED, which represents powder density associated with displaced volume. Fine powders showed increasing feed rate and continuous densification during feeding, whereas di-calcium phosphate and CapsuLac60 showed an initial expansion followed by densification. For preconditioned cartridges, average ρ*ED should equal 1, although local values could initially be below tapped density and later exceed it. The excerpt reports feed rates of 1.5–15 g/h and deviations of no more than 10–20% at constant piston speed. It does not describe prediction of particle size as an output, nor provide a quantitative size-to-feed-rate correlation here. Important caveats include density gradients, wall-friction-induced densification, preconditioning effects, and unavailable FT4 data for silicon dioxide.

contexts.context: This excerpt primarily supports the 2021 controlled continuous low-dose feeding paper, not the 2020 performance-evaluation or 2024 densification papers. It describes direct gravimetric measurement in conventional loss-in-weight feeding as monitoring the feeder mass with a balance beneath the feeding unit. The micro-feeder itself is volumetric: it delivers a constant powder volume per unit time, while the effective mass feed rate depends on powder displacement density. Density changes during feeding are therefore characterized using a displacement feed factor (effective displacement density) profile for each material, and that profile is used in feed-forward control to adjust powder displacement rate and maintain the target mass feed rate. Particle sizes are not reported as numerical measurements for all materials in this excerpt; they are described qualitatively as a large-particle di-calcium phosphate system, a small-particle croscarmellose sodium system, and very small barium sulfate particles below 10 μm. The cited prediction concerns feed rate at set points, not particle size as an output. No quantitative correlation between particle size and displacement density/feed-factor changes is provided on these pages. Relevant caveats include material-dependent density variation, cohesion and low density, and the difficulty of low-rate feeding caused by screw fluctuations, hopper refilling, powder-bed-height changes, bridging, and adhesion.

contexts.context: The excerpt is relevant only to Dai and Grace (2011), not to the Allenspach 2021 HPMC LIW feeder, Jaspers 2025 batch variability, Kobayashi 2024 feed-factor profile, or Bostijn 2019. Dai and Grace independently varied or examined biomass particle mean size over 0.5–15 mm, size distribution, shape, moisture content from 10–60%, density, and compressibility. The reported output framework is a volumetric feed rate and derived mass flow rate rather than a size-based prediction: V = A v ηv, where A is screw cross-sectional area, v is ideal axial velocity (uP/2π), and ηv is volumetric efficiency; mass flow is M = V ρb, using bulk density. It identifies the choke section and seal plug as important determinants of torque. The equations relate feeder geometry, speed, volumetric efficiency, and bulk density to throughput, not inverse estimation of size.

contexts.context: Hou (2024) indicates that particle size and cohesion affect dosing indirectly through powder flowability. In rotary valves, poor flowability can produce bridging and ratholing, so the device is generally restricted to easy-flowing materials; rotor speed regulates the flow rate, while rotor and housing geometry determine transfer through the inlet and outlet. The commercial-feeder table shows that operating ranges span micrometre-to-millimetre particles and widely varying bulk densities, with particular devices aimed at fine, cohesive, wet, or low-flow powders. Bulk density is therefore a key specification rather than a universal limit: examples include powders around 0.14–0.783 kg/dm³ and micronised calcium carbonate below 0.16 kg/dm³. Moisture and cohesion are explicitly associated with the DEC µPTS application, whereas the excerpt does not provide a general moisture model. Venturi feeders avoid moving parts but have fixed geometry, potentially limiting feed-rate range; air velocity can cause abrasive wear and particle degradation, changing particle size and shape and thereby affecting consistency. The excerpt describes gravimetric vibratory and loss-in-weight commercial systems, but it does not state that particle size or PSD is estimated as an output from gravimetric mass-time traces, nor does it detail feedback-control algorithms. contexts.context: The Yang and Evans excerpt establishes a clear particle-size dependence for dosing, but specifically for narrow particle-size-distribution (PSD) fractions: in a given tube, dose was inversely proportional to particle size. It also gives a geometric constraint for valve operation: the orifice-radius/particle-radius ratio should lie between 2 and 5. Capillary geometry is important more generally, since flow rate was highly sensitive to capillary diameter; ultrasonic systems used capillaries from 50 μm to 1.3 mm and achieved doses down to 10 μg or flow rates near 10 μg s−1. The reported flow mechanisms involve wall friction, particle arrest, stasis and re-initiation, and an ultrasonically vibrated powder layer that can act as a lubricant. Cohesive or arching behavior is indicated by domes forming in an unvibrated tube, requiring an attack waveform to break them. The excerpt does not report estimating particle size or PSD as an output from gravimetric mass-versus-time traces; it instead treats particle size, PSD, vibration, and geometry as inputs or operating parameters. It states that finer powders, particularly those below approximately 50–100 μm, develop stronger cohesive, electrostatic, van der Waals, and capillary interactions, causing agglomeration and wall adhesion. contexts.context: The excerpt does not specifically discuss Yang and Evans (2007) or Hou (2024), nor does it establish a particle-size-dependent dosing law or show that particle size/PSD can be estimated as an output from gravimetric mass-time traces. It does, however, provide relevant constraints for interpreting dosing performance. Powder cohesion and aggregation produce flow-rate fluctuations even when the mean rate is constant, while changes in bulk density can decouple volumetric delivery from mass feedrate. Density varies with consolidation, moisture, particle size, segregation, and attrition; therefore, volumetric feeding requires density stability, whereas gravimetric/loss-in-weight control compensates for density changes by feedback. Feeder performance also depends on the selected hopper, flow aids, weighing platform, and dispensing mechanism, with screw, vibration, belt, and rotary-valve mechanisms identified. In loss-in-weight operation, the hopper and feeder are weighed over time; the controller calculates feedrate from the change in measured mass divided by time and adjusts the dispensing mechanism toward the setpoint. Thus, mass-time traces directly support feedrate estimation and control, but the excerpt gives no basis for uniquely inferring particle size or PSD from those traces. Such inference would require an independently validated relationship separating particle-size effects from density, moisture, cohesion, consolidation, geometry, and feedback dynamics.

contexts.context: The excerpt does not discuss Torres-Serra et al. (2021) directly, nor does it define that study’s model features and labels or explain whether gravimetric feeding traces alone are used to predict particle size or particle-size distribution (PSD). It does, however, show that particle-size information is represented by dv50, defined as the 50% cumulative undersize of the volumetric distribution, and that this quantity is obtained using laser diffraction. Other material-property variables are separately characterized using a tapping device and pycnometer—bulk density, tapped density, Hausner ratio, Carr index, true density, and porosity—and a ring shear tester, which provides flow-function and stress-related descriptors such as ffc, unconfined yield strength, major principal stress, and bulk-density-weighed flow. Thus, within this excerpt, size and flow properties are measured material descriptors rather than quantities extracted from feeding mass-time traces. The excerpt also notes that the presented multivariate models assume linear relationships and suggests investigating nonlinear modeling approaches. It provides no evidence about the specific training-data instruments or label definitions in the Torres-Serra paper, so those details cannot be reliably determined from the supplied text.

contexts.context: Bostijn et al. (2019) studied 15 pharmaceutical powders using a low-feed-rate twin-screw/loss-in-weight feeder. In gravimetric mode, feed rate was calculated as consecutive balance mass differences divided by time differences, while screw speed was adjusted to maintain setpoint. They measured feed-rate variability (RSD) and relative error (RE), and used 25 material-property descriptors—including particle-characterization data—to predict these responses with PLS regression. The models predicted feeding behavior, but the excerpt reports no inference of particle size or particle-size distribution from mass-versus-time, fluctuations, or mass per screw revolution.

contexts.context: The excerpt concerns prediction of feeder behavior from raw-material-property descriptors, rather than prediction of particle-size distribution (PSD). The feed-factor profile is used to derive two volumetric feeding responses: maximum feed factor (FFmax) and feed-factor decay (FFdecay). These responses, together with gravimetric responses such as relative standard deviation (RSD) and relative error (RE), are modeled using PLS models based on measured powder properties. The reported model outputs are therefore feeding-performance quantities, expressed as mass per revolution for FFmax at different screw speeds and as percentage decay for FFdecay—not PSD descriptors. The validation table compares actual and predicted feeding responses for powders, reinforcing that the prediction direction is from material-property inputs to feeder-response outputs. Although the excerpt does not specify the Kobayashi et al. (2024) model or identify its exact measured PSD descriptor, it supports an important distinction: mass per revolution is a feed-factor/volumetric-feeding response and should not be interpreted as a prediction of PSD. If a two-component mixed-powder model uses component fractions and process/material properties as inputs, its output is most naturally the feed-factor profile or its parameters. A PSD descriptor would be a separate measured target unless the model explicitly defines PSD as the dependent variable.
contexts.question: In Kobayashi et al 2024 Feed factor profile prediction model for two-component mixed powder in the twin-screw feeder, what is the direction of prediction and measured PSD descriptor? Explain if mass per revolution predicts PSD or only profile of feed factor; model input fraction process material properties.

contexts.context: The excerpt discusses predicting feeder performance from material flow properties using PCA and PLSR, but it does not address Kobayashi et al. (2024), particle-size-distribution (PSD) descriptors, or the direction of prediction between mass per revolution and PSD. Its relevant distinction is that a strong correlation was observed between material-property-derived principal-component scores and the initial feed factor, which represents the maximum capacity of a screw. The text states that material properties can therefore be used to estimate the initial feed factor and define the operating space, especially when material quantity is limited. It also describes a workflow in which a new material’s flow properties are characterized and compared with existing materials to predict an optimal screw. However, this excerpt provides no evidence that mass per revolution predicts PSD, nor does it establish whether such a model predicts a PSD descriptor or only the feed-factor profile. It likewise does not specify model inputs based on component fraction or process-material properties in the two-component mixed-powder context.

contexts.context: This excerpt does not describe Kobayashi et al. (2024) or establish the specific prediction direction in that paper. It does, however, clarify a relevant modeling distinction: particle-size descriptors (d10, d50, and d90) are treated as material-property inputs, alongside bulk density, compressibility, permeability, shear-cell, and dynamic-flow properties, for predicting feeder performance. The feeder-performance response is characterized by actual mass feed rate and its relationship to the target, including consistency (RSD) and deviation from the set point (RDM), rather than by directly predicting particle-size distribution from feeder output. The excerpt therefore supports interpreting mass-per-revolution or feed-factor measurements as feeder/process responses. Such measurements may be used to predict or characterize the profile of feed factor (or feeder performance) as operating conditions or composition change; they are not shown here as a direct predictor of PSD itself. For the two-component mixed-powder question, the relevant direction should be checked in Kobayashi et al.: whether the model maps composition/process/material properties to feed-factor profile, or inversely maps mass-per-revolution to a PSD descriptor. This excerpt indicates that multivariate models such as PLSR can regress material-property inputs to feeder performance, but it provides no evidence for an inverse mass-per-revolution-to-PSD model.

contexts.context: This excerpt describes feed-factor profiling in a twin-screw feeder, but it does not report the Kobayashi et al. (2024) two-component mixed-powder prediction model, its prediction direction, or a measured particle-size-distribution (PSD) descriptor. Here, the feed factor is defined as powder mass dispensed per screw revolution (g/revolution), calculated from the measured catch-scale feed rate and screw speed. The experiments generate a feed-factor profile as a function of hopper fill level at fixed screw speeds, and extract FFmax and FFdecay. Thus, within this methodology, mass per revolution is an output/response used to characterize or predict feeder feeding behavior; it is not presented as a PSD measurement and does not by itself establish prediction of PSD. The excerpt also indicates that material density affects comparison of profiles, so hopper mass is normalized into a percentage fill level. Material-specific behavior is evaluated across different powders, but no model inputs involving component fraction, process-material properties, or PSD descriptors are specified here. Consequently, this source can support the distinction that feed factor concerns feeder performance/profile, while it cannot determine whether the 2024 model predicts PSD from mass per revolution, predicts feed factor from PSD and material fractions, or uses a measured PSD descriptor in either direction.

contexts.context: Kobayashi et al. measure particle-size-distribution descriptors D10, D50, and D90, defined as the particle diameters below which 10%, 50%, and 90% of particles fall, respectively. However, these PSD descriptors are material-property measurements used as inputs or characterization variables; the prediction target is not PSD. The modeled quantity is the feed factor, f, calculated as instantaneous flow rate F divided by screw rotation speed ω (equivalently, mass per revolution). The models therefore predict the feed-factor value/profile as a function of hopper powder weight and other experimental/material variables, rather than predicting D10, D50, or D90 from mass per revolution. The candidate input-variable groups include powder weight in the hopper (W), screw rotation speed (ω), ethenzamide mass fraction (XAPI), and measured material properties (Props). The material properties include PSD descriptors among other powder properties, so PSD can inform feed-factor prediction when included in a variable group, but the study does not establish that feed factor or mass per revolution predicts PSD. The physical model specifically describes the nonlinear relationship between feed factor and powder weight in the hopper; alternative data-driven and gray-box models incorporate fraction, operating speed, and material-property information.

contexts.context: The Yang and Evans review provides limited but relevant support for linking powder-feeding behavior to particle size. It reports that, for narrow particle-size-distribution fractions dispensed through a given tube, dose was inversely proportional to particle size. This is the closest explicit particle-size/feeding-mass relationship in the excerpt and could motivate a powder-specific calibration, but it is not presented as a general quantitative correlation suitable for inferring size from arbitrary feeding traces. The review emphasizes that discharged mass is also governed by vibration amplitude, acceleration, particle kinetic energy, capillary or orifice dimensions, frequency, and wall-friction effects. In ultrasonic capillary feeding, flow rate was highly sensitive to capillary diameter and power, with a vibrating powder layer near the wall acting as a lubricant. The cited ultrasonic systems reached approximately 10 μg/s for powders around 3 μm, while individual tungsten-carbide doses as low as 50 μg were obtained. These observations indicate that distinct fed-mass fluctuations or flow trends may reflect particle size, but they are confounded by apparatus and operating parameters. The excerpt contains no FF metric, no time-resolved fluctuation analysis, and no regression or calibration curve of particle size versus FF. Thus, it offers qualitative mechanistic guidance and one inverse dose-size relationship, rather than validated evidence for a universal PSD-independent particle-size proxy.

contexts.context: This Bostijn et al. excerpt provides indirect evidence that particle size can influence feeding-trace behavior, but it does not establish a calibrated particle-size proxy from feed-factor (FF) data. In the gravimetric feeding model, powders with small particle size were associated with greater feed-rate variability when combined with low density, poor flow, and high compressibility; the proposed mechanism was inconsistent screw filling. For FFmax, however, density and powder flow were identified as the material properties with the largest impact. The excerpt gives a concrete contrast between lactose (CL) and PH105: despite similar bulk density, CL had higher FFmax, attributed to better flow. FFdecay was primarily associated with compressibility, while flow and density were negatively correlated with FFdecay. No quantitative particle-size-versus-FF correlation, regression coefficient, controlled particle-size-fraction experiment, or distinct FF trend attributable specifically to particle size is reported in these pages. Particle size appears as one descriptor within a multivariate model and is confounded with other powder properties. Thus, this source may support particle size as a potentially relevant covariate for powder-specific modeling of variability, but not as evidence for replacing PSD measurements with a universally calibrated size proxy. Additional studies with experimentally separated size fractions and independently reported FF trajectories would be needed.

contexts.context: This excerpt does not report original experiments in which particle-size fractions were deliberately varied, nor does it document particle-size-specific fed-mass fluctuations or feed-factor (FF) trends. Its quantitative relationships concern bulk powder properties and feeding performance instead. Bulk density increased linearly with the maximum feed factor, while tapped bulk density increased linearly with the change in feed factor (FFmax − FFmin). Flow-rate variability decreased exponentially as flow-function coefficient (FFC) increased, with FFC values above 3 associated with less than 1% flow-rate variability. The excerpt also identifies conditioned bulk density (cBD) as having the strongest correlation with regressed feed-factor parameters, and notes that compressibility at 15 kPa correlated strongly with minimum feed factor. These findings could support a calibrated, powder-specific feeding proxy based on density, compressibility, or cohesion, but they do not establish a quantitative particle-size-versus-FF relationship. Particle size is therefore not separable from other powder characteristics in the reported correlations, and the passage cannot support using feeding traces alone to infer particle size or PSD. The named studies in the question (Fathollahi, Jaspers, Bostijn, Allenspach, and Yang) are not discussed in this excerpt.

contexts.context: This excerpt from Bostijn et al. establishes a useful experimental framework for assessing whether particle size can be inferred from feeder traces, but it does not provide the needed quantitative particle-size/feeding correlations. Particle size was directly measured by laser diffraction and represented by dv50, the 50% cumulative undersize of the volumetric particle-size distribution; measurements were performed in triplicate. Separately, volumetric feeding responses were characterized as FFmax and FFdecay at screw speeds of 6, 30, and 54 rpm for each powder. The study also measured gravimetric variability and error at 0.1 and 0.55 kg/h, although those metrics are not particle-size correlations in this excerpt. Thus, Bostijn supports pairing an experimentally measured size descriptor such as dv50 with feed-factor responses across powders and screw speeds. However, these pages describe methods only: they do not document experimentally varied particle-size fractions, distinct fed-mass fluctuation patterns attributable specifically to size, regression coefficients, or a calibrated powder-specific size proxy based on FF. Results from the cited Fathollahi, Jaspers, Allenspach, and Yang studies would be needed to determine whether such correlations exist.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides qualitative evidence that particle size can affect powder feeding, but it does not report experimentally isolated particle-size fractions, fed-mass fluctuation signatures, or a quantitative particle-size-versus-feed-factor (FF) correlation. Pharmatose® 350 M has the smallest particle size and reduced flowability and consistently produces the lowest FF, which is attributed to less efficient screw filling. However, the two Pharmatose® 200 M grades have nearly identical particle-size distributions while showing different feeding behavior in stretched and low-feed-rate configurations. This indicates that particle size alone is insufficient and that other properties—such as flowability, bulk density, moisture, and possibly surface characteristics—contribute to FF. The PCA analysis of 435 batches includes particle size among variables associated with PC1 and PC2, but the first two components explain only 30% of total variation and are described as having limited predictive power. Thus, within this excerpt, there is no calibrated powder-specific size proxy derived from feeding traces, nor evidence that FF trends uniquely encode particle size independently of other material properties and feeder configuration. The cited results support particle size as a potentially relevant covariate, not as a standalone quantitative predictor.

contexts.context: This excerpt from Allenspach et al. provides indirect evidence relevant to using feeding traces as a powder-property proxy, but it does not establish a calibrated particle-size-versus-feeding-fluctuation (FF) relationship. The authors note that particle size, along with bulk density and particle shape, can affect the screw speed needed to obtain a target mass flow. However, the reported comparison is between directly compressed (DC) and conventionally granulated (CR) HPMC grades, rather than experimentally varied particle-size fractions. DC materials showed lower mass-flow standard deviations and lower mean instantaneous mass-flow RSD than CR materials, indicating that feeding-trace variability can distinguish material types or processing states. The excerpt also identifies several non-size-specific causes of excursions, including hopper refills, external scale disturbances, material-property changes, electrostatic adhesion, buildup at the screw outlet, and subsequent material drop-off. Ratholing and failed refills were observed for some CR grades. Thus, the work supports FF as a sensitive operational signal, but the fluctuations cannot be uniquely attributed to particle size without controlling for electrostatics, density, flowability, refill behavior, and feeder conditions. No quantitative correlation or particle-size calibration is reported in this excerpt.

contexts.context: Fathollahi et al. provide a qualitative basis for interpreting particle size from powder-feeding traces, but the excerpt does not establish a calibrated, powder-specific particle-size proxy or a quantitative particle-size-versus-feed-fluctuation (FF) correlation. The study compares several materials with substantially different particle-size distributions and reports that larger-particle, lower-compressibility powders initially produce higher feed rates and stronger initial densification, whereas finer, more compressible powders densify only slightly. CapsuLac60 and dicalcium phosphate show a distinctive nonmonotonic trace: feed rate decreases initially to a minimum and then rises, unlike the finer powders. However, feeding behavior is explicitly attributed to multiple coupled properties—particle-size distribution, bulk density, compressibility, and elastic behavior—so particle size cannot be isolated as the causal predictor. The excerpt reports material-level trends rather than experiments in which particle-size fractions were systematically varied within one powder and their fed-mass fluctuations quantified. It also does not provide regression coefficients, sensitivity values, or an FF metric linked independently to particle size. Thus, this paper can support hypothesis generation and qualitative classification of trace shapes, but not a validated size estimator independent of PSD and powder rheology.

contexts.context: This excerpt from Bostijn et al. is relevant for defining and extracting powder-feeding trace features, but it does not provide a direct particle-size calibration. The study tested 15 distinct pharmaceutical raw materials, including dense, powder, and micronized paracetamol/API categories, so these materials may offer qualitative contrasts associated with particle size. However, the excerpt does not state that particle-size fractions of the same material were experimentally prepared or varied systematically; the powders appear to be separate commercial/raw-material identities. Volumetric feeding was conducted at 6, 30, and 54 rpm, with feed rate recorded every second using a catch scale. The resulting feed-factor profile plots feed factor (mass per screw revolution) against hopper fill level. Two extracted descriptors are especially relevant as potential powder-specific trace proxies: FFmax, the maximum observed feed factor and a measure of feeding capacity, and FFdecay, the hopper-fill level at which feed factor falls to 90% of FFmax. The excerpt documents a general decrease in feed factor as hopper fill decreases, but it gives no quantitative correlation between particle size and FFmax, FFdecay, fluctuation magnitude, or another trace statistic. Thus, Bostijn supports a methodology for deriving calibrated, material-specific feeding signatures, but not a validated particle-size proxy independent of PSD. Establishing such a proxy would require within-material size-fraction experiments and reported statistical correlations.

answer.formatted_answer:
Question: Has anyone inferred or predicted the particle size or particle size distribution of a powder from gravimetric dispensing or feeding data, that is, from balance mass-versus-time readings, mass-flow-rate fluctuations, or the mass delivered per screw revolution of a screw/auger feeder, loss-in-weight feeder or automated powder dosing instrument?


No. ## Finding

**I did not find a published, validated demonstration that predicts a powder’s particle size or particle-size distribution (PSD) *from gravimetric feeder or dispenser data alone***—whether balance mass-versus-time readings, fluctuations in the derived mass-flow rate, or mass delivered per screw revolution. This is a qualified literature-search finding, not proof that no such method exists. The closest studies establish that particle size *affects* feeding, or use feeder signals to infer packing and equipment behavior, but they do not report size or PSD as the predicted output. (bostijn2019amultivariateapproach pages 1-6, fathollahi2020performanceevaluationof pages 1-2, fathollahi2024understandingpowderbehavior pages 3-5, kobayashi2024feedfactorprofile pages 3-4)

The distinction between what was measured and what was predicted is central:

| Study | Feeder-derived measurement | Actual size-related role / conclusion |
|---|---|---|
| Bostijn et al. (2019) | Feed-factor maximum and decay (`FFmax`, `FFdecay`), plus gravimetric feed-rate variability and relative error (`RSD`, `RE`) | Laser-diffraction `dv50` was an independently measured input used to predict feeder responses—not an output inferred from gravimetry. (bostijn2019amultivariateapproach pages 1-6, bostijn2019amultivariateapproach pages 14-18) |
| Fathollahi et al. (2020) | Catch-balance discharged mass at 1 s intervals and a displacement-feed-factor profile characterizing effective-density changes | Particle size was measured separately by laser diffraction. Trace differences were associated jointly with size, compressibility, packing, and density; PSD was not predicted from the balance trace. (fathollahi2020performanceevaluationof pages 4-5, fathollahi2020performanceevaluationof pages 5-7) |
| Fathollahi et al. (2024) | LIW data at 1 Hz; feed factor in g/rev, with local and overall trends used to indicate densification and screw layering | PSD was measured separately by dry laser diffraction. Feed-factor trends diagnose feeder phenomena, not particle size or PSD. (fathollahi2024understandingpowderbehavior pages 3-5, fathollahi2024understandingpowderbehavior pages 8-10, fathollahi2024understandingpowderbehavior media b6404b79) |
| Kobayashi et al. (2024) | Feed-factor profile—mass delivered per screw rotation as a function of hopper powder weight | Models predict the feed-factor profile from hopper weight, API fraction, screw speed, and optionally independently measured properties including `D10`, `D50`, and `D90`; they do not invert feed factor to obtain PSD. (kobayashi2024feedfactorprofile pages 1-2, kobayashi2024feedfactorprofile pages 3-4, kobayashi2024feedfactorprofile pages 2-3) |
| Jaspers et al. (2025) | Feed factor under different feeder configurations | The finest lactose grade had the lowest feed factor, but grades with nearly identical PSDs behaved differently, showing that size is not uniquely recoverable from feed factor. (jaspers2025optimizingcontinuousfeeding pages 5-8) |
| Archary et al. (2016) | Feeder speed/feed factor supported coal mass-flow estimation | Online PSD/fineness came from a separate laser particle-size probe and was validated against sampling and sieving—not inferred from feeder gravimetry. (archary2016massflowand pages 13-16, archary2016massflowand pages 20-22, archary2016massflowand pages 1-3) |
| **Overall finding** | **Balance mass-time, mass-flow fluctuations, or mass per revolution** | **None of these studies predicts particle size or PSD from feeder gravimetry; size is independently measured, used as an input/covariate, or obtained from a separate optical sensor.** |


*Table: The closest published studies use particle size as an independently measured input or infer feeder phenomena such as density change and screw layering. None of the listed studies reconstructs particle size or PSD from gravimetric feeder data alone.*

**The closest signal-based inference** is Fathollahi and colleagues’ 2024 loss-in-weight study. They logged hopper weight, mass flow, screw speed, and *feed factor*—grams delivered per revolution—at 1 Hz. Changes in the feed-factor profile were interpreted as evidence of powder densification within feeding cycles and powder layering on the screws across cycles. PSD, however, was measured separately by laser diffraction, not reconstructed from that profile. Their Figure 4 illustrates the two feed-factor trends used for those *operational* diagnoses. (fathollahi2024understandingpowderbehavior pages 3-5, fathollahi2024understandingpowderbehavior pages 8-10, fathollahi2024understandingpowderbehavior media b6404b79)

**There is a plausible size signal, but not a demonstrated inverse estimator.** In a micro-feeder study with an outlet balance, finer and more compressible powders generally showed different effective-density and feeding trajectories from coarser powders; the authors used the gravimetric data to characterize density variation and improve feed-rate prediction, not to estimate size. In a lactose-feeding comparison, the finest grade had the lowest feed factor, yet two grades with nearly identical PSDs also fed differently under some configurations. An earlier dispensing review reported an inverse relationship between dose and particle size for *narrow size fractions in a particular tube*, but did not turn that relationship into a general, validated balance-trace-to-PSD method. (fathollahi2020performanceevaluationof pages 4-5, fathollahi2020performanceevaluationof pages 1-2, fathollahi2020performanceevaluationof pages 5-7, jaspers2025optimizingcontinuousfeeding pages 5-8, yang2007meteringanddispensing pages 9-10)

**Why mass per revolution is not itself a size measurement.** If screw geometry is fixed, mass delivered per revolution reflects how much of its available volume the powder fills *and the density of that filled powder*. Both can change with hopper level, consolidation, flowability, cohesion, adhesion to the screws, and operating conditions. In gravimetric mode, feedback also changes screw speed to hold mass flow near its setpoint, potentially suppressing differences in the flow-rate trace while leaving differences in feed factor. Consequently, different PSDs can plausibly yield similar signals, and similar PSDs can yield different signals; a full PSD is especially difficult to identify uniquely from one aggregate mass measurement. This is an inference from the reported feeder physics and comparisons, not an experimentally proven impossibility. (engisch2014lossinweightfeedingin pages 22-27, bostijn2019amultivariateapproach pages 22-26, fathollahi2024understandingpowderbehavior pages 8-10, jaspers2025optimizingcontinuousfeeding pages 5-8)

A **powder- and instrument-specific classifier or estimate of a limited size statistic**, such as a change in median size or fines content, remains a reasonable research hypothesis. Demonstrating it would require independently measured PSD labels for systematically varied size fractions of the *same material*, synchronized balance and screw-speed records, controlled density/moisture/fill-level and operating conditions, and validation on held-out batches. Existing studies provide candidate trace features—feed-factor level and decay, cycle trends, and feed-rate variability—but do **not** establish the accuracy or generalizability of such an inverse model. Where actual online fineness was reported alongside feeder-derived flow information in a pulverized-fuel study, the size measurement came instead from a separate optical particle-size probe. (bostijn2019amultivariateapproach pages 10-14, bostijn2019amultivariateapproach pages 14-18, fathollahi2024understandingpowderbehavior pages 8-10, archary2016massflowand pages 13-16, archary2016massflowand pages 1-3)
